en: Mātṛkā 1 [Legal Procedure]:
When men were solely devoted to Dharma and speakers of truth;

At that time, there was no legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), nor hatred, nor even envy. When dharma had perished among human beings, legal procedure came into being; and the king was appointed as the upholder of the rod of punishment and the arbiter of legal procedures.
In this regard, two methods are proclaimed: written evidence and witnesses.
For the purpose of clarifying a disputed matter between two contending parties, that [evidence] should be understood as having two characteristics:
with a reply and without a reply.
NM 1.4c: "With a counter-stake" (*sottara*) means where there is a wager preceded by a written contract (*vilekhā*).
NM 1.5a–c: In a dispute involving a counter-stake, whichever of the two parties loses therein, he shall be made to pay the stake he himself undertook, as well as the fine for defeat.
The essence of legal proceedings is declared to be the plaint;
if that is abandoned, the proponent loses, while he who crosses over it becomes the respondent.
Families, guilds, assemblies, officials, and the king [are the authorities].
The foundation of legal procedures rests upon these [authorities], each succeeding one being more authoritative than the preceding.
It is proclaimed as having four feet, four bases, and four means; it is beneficial in four ways, pervasive in four ways, and accomplishes four purposes.

It has eight limbs and eighteen titles; likewise, it has a hundred branches. It has three origins, two types of legal proceedings, two doors, and two destinies. Furthermore, it consists of Dharma, judicial procedure, custom, and royal edict.
This four-footed legal procedure consists of the subsequent [claim] which subverts the prior.
Among these, *dharma* (the truth) is established in the case of truth; *vyavahāra* (legal procedure) rests upon witnesses;
*caritra* (customary practice) resides in written records; and *śāsana* (the royal edict) lies in the king’s command.
Because it is to be accomplished through the means of conciliation and the rest, it is called "having four instruments" (*catuḥsādhana*);

and because it protects the four stages of life (*āśrama*), it is "beneficial to the four" (*caturhita*). Furthermore, [it concerns] the litigants, the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king.
Because it pervades [the four goals] quarter by quarter, it is therefore remembered as "four-pervading" (caturvyāpin).
Because it accomplishes these four— dharma, artha, fame, and likewise public esteem—
it is proclaimed as "four-effecting" (catuṣkārī).
The king, his officers, the members of the court, the legal treatise, the calculator, and the scribe;
gold, fire, and water—this is declared to be the eightfold limb [of the court].
Indeed, non-payment of debt, deposits, and partnership are [the first topics].

Taking back what has been given, failing to perform service after having entered into an agreement, non-payment of wages, as well as sale by one who is not the owner, failure to deliver after having sold, and likewise regret after having purchased; 17.
The non-performance of agreements, disputes concerning land,
the relationship between husband and wife, partition of inheritance,
and then violence; verbal abuse, as well as physical assault, have been thus declared.
Gambling and miscellaneous matters—thus the law is remembered as having eighteen titles (padas).
Another division of these very titles is recorded as one hundred and eight;
it is described as having a hundred branches due to the diversity of human actions.

Because it proceeds from three sources—desire, anger, and greed—it is proclaimed to have three origins; therefore, this triad is the cause of disputes. Furthermore, a lawsuit should be understood as being of two kinds: based on suspicion and based on the actual facts.
But the doubt regarding the non-existent arises from association with the wicked, as seen in cases such as the "carried-away" [woman].
Because it is connected to two sides, it is described as having two doors:
of those two, the first position is the *pakṣa* (proposition), and the counter-position is the *uttara* (reply).

Because it follows both reality and deception, that [chala] is said to have two courses. Reality (bhūta) is that which is conjoined with the true meaning; deception (chala) is that which is stated through negligence.
In that regard, the king who employs righteousness as his instrument should tolerate the remaining [type of] deception.
One should resort only to what is factual, for prosperity has its root in dharma.
For a king who is self-disciplined and adjudicates legal cases according to dharma,
seven virtues arise, like the seven flames of fire.
Dharma, wealth, fame, the ripening of the world, the winning over of others, great respect from his subjects, and an eternal station in heaven— therefore,
having ascended the seat of justice, the king, free from envy, [should act accordingly].
He should be impartial toward all living beings, upholding the law of Yama;
placing the treatises on Dharma before him and abiding by the opinion of the presiding judge, he should examine the legal cases with a concentrated mind in their proper order.

First, the traditional authority (*āgama*) should be applied, and then the subject matter of the legal dispute (*vyavahārapada*); furthermore, the desire to know and the final decision—thus, the judicial process (*darśana*) is fourfold.
One should proceed according to the path without contradiction between the treatises on Dharma and the treatises on worldly affairs (*artha*).

Examining it skillfully, he should lead the course of the legal proceeding. Just as a hunter, when a deer has been wounded, follows the track of the deer by means of a trace of blood in the undergrowth, so should he follow the path of justice.
Where there may be a conflict between the *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Arthaśāstra*,
one should set aside what is stated in the *Arthaśāstra* and practice what is stated in the *Dharmaśāstra*. However,
in the event of a contradiction with the *Dharmaśāstra*, even that which is supported by reasoning is not [in accordance] with *dharma*.
For legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is powerful; by it, Dharma is set aside.
(34) For the blessed Dharma is subtle, beyond the senses, and difficult to discern.
Therefore, one should lead the course of legal procedure by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (35)
Even one who is not a thief incurs the status of a thief, and a thief attains the status of a non-thief;
through legal proceedings, Māṇḍavya—who was not a thief—attained the status of a thief.
[Likewise, one may be accused] regarding women, at night, outside the village, inside a house, or in the presence of enemies.
Even if a legal proceeding has been concluded regarding these matters, it may be reopened.
Because of the complexity of disputes and the potential failure of memory,
one may take time at will in cases such as debts when there is a desire to ascertain the truth.

In cases of theft of cattle, land, gold, or women; in cases of assault and violence; in matters of urgency; in acts of force; and in cases of false accusation, one should initiate a lawsuit immediately. But he who proceeds with a disputed matter without having reported it to the king [is at fault].
He should be restrained by force; yet his purpose is not accomplished.
One who seeks a legal dispute should detain a person who does not abide by what is to be said and who evades those words, until the appearance for summons.
Confinement may be of four kinds: by place, by time, by exile, and likewise by labor. One must not violate such confinement while it remains unexpired.
[This applies] in cases such as crossing rivers, traversing wildernesses, or being beset by difficult terrain or calamities.

One who, while being under a stay-at-home order (*āsiddha*), departs from that restriction does not commit an offense. However, he who violates the stay-at-home order during the period when it is in effect must be punished;
by acting otherwise, the person under the order becomes liable for a fine, whereas the one who imposed the order shall incur the penalty.
One who desires to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one beset by calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in royal service;
herdsmen while tending cattle, and farmers while binding the crops. (45–46a)

Artisans, as well as those bearing arms during a conflict, are not to be summoned at that time. Furthermore, one who has not yet attained legal majority, an envoy, one intent on giving a gift, one under a religious vow, and one in a precarious situation must not be obstructed, nor shall the king summon them.
One who is not himself formally accused should not bring an accusation against another; nor, having failed to settle that matter, should he do so by another means.
Furthermore, one who has been accused by another does not deserve to strike back at him.
Whatever matter one brings as an accusation, one should not subject it to improper treatment.
He should not resort to another alternative plea; by doing so, he is defeated relative to his previous position.

(49) One should not bring a false accusation; the fault belongs to the one who makes a false accusation. Whatever punishment has been prescribed for that [offense] shall apply to the accuser as well. (50)
One who evades the time for trial by using pretexts, one who remains silent in the assembly,

one who speaks after having already spoken, and one who contradicts what was said— these are the characteristics of one who is losing the case. Furthermore, he who flees when summoned and he who does not appear for the lawsuit when it has arrived [are also so characterized].

That person should be punished by the king and indeed excluded from the legal proceeding (52). In cases where a lawsuit has been adjudicated, documentary evidence or witnesses shall be rendered fruitless if they were not previously presented (53).
Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grains have already ripened,
so too is evidence useless for those whose legal proceedings have been concluded.
Even that which is untrue, if stated at the appropriate time, is examined.
But that which, through negligence, is not stated, even if it be true, is lost.
If anyone should consider a case already decided and adjudicated to be contrary to the law,
one should impose a double fine and reopen that matter.
But when a legal proceeding has been wrongly decided, the members of the court shall incur that same punishment;
for indeed, no one ever remains on the path of righteousness without the threat of punishment.
He who speaks otherwise, whether out of passion, ignorance, or greed, [shall be punished].
He who is a member of the assembly but acts unseemly should be recognized as such, and the king should severely punish him.
However, by the king especially, while guarding his own duty,
the quality of being virtuous or non-virtuous must be examined due to the diversity of human minds.

There are men who, out of greed, might give false testimony; there are also other evil-minded people who forge documents. Therefore, the king must especially examine both of these matters with great care.
A document is [validated] by the conduct regarding documents, and witnesses by the conduct regarding witnesses.
(61) Untruths appear like truths, and truths appear as untruths;
various states of affairs are seen in this way. Therefore, careful examination is necessary. (62)
The sky appears like a surface, and a firefly like a flame;
yet there is no surface in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly.
Therefore, even that which is perceived through direct perception ought to be examined for its true nature.

By investigating and making known the facts of a case, a king does not fall away from dharma. Seeing matters in this way, a king who is always composed while presiding over legal proceedings spreads his radiant glory here and attains the realm of the Sun.
Mātṛkā 2 (Mātṛkā 2 is found only in manuscript P) [The second chapter of the Mātṛkā included in Jolly’s edition and translation is not part of the original Nāradasmṛti].
(See the Introduction to the text). Its translation is provided in the Appendix.
[vernacular]
Having gained the strength of firm conviction, the plaintiff, impelled by his own interest and having reached a certainty regarding the matter to be accomplished,
shall cause the *pūrvapakṣa* (the initial plea) to be written down.
Thereafter, the defendant, having heard the meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa*, [shall respond].
One should set forth the counter-argument connected to the meaning of the plaintiff's case. The defendant may obtain a period for writing his response of one day, three days, or even seven days.
However, if the plaintiff is established in the third stage of the process, he is certainly victorious immediately.
The reply (uttara) may be of four kinds: a false admission, a counter-attack, a plea for a prior judgment, or a plea based on a previous legal proceeding.
"This is false," "I do not recognize it," "I was not present there at that time."

And at that very time, I am unborn; thus, the false is of four kinds. (NM 2.5) The false, the perverted, and furthermore, that which conforms to the sound [of the words], and that which is connected to the meaning of the prima facie argument—thus the rejoinder is of four kinds. (NM 2.6)
The plaintiff shall cause the defendant to submit a reply to his statement only so long as the matter intended to be expressed has not been fully set forth.
A petition that is for another purpose, devoid of meaning, or lacking in proof and scriptural authority [is inadmissible].
A document that is deficient or excessive, or one that is corrupted—these are declared to be defects of the plaint (bhāṣā-doṣa).
Whatever is to be obtained by whom, from whom, and what—that person shall receive that from him;
but not another thing from another source. Thus, this "other matter" (anyārtha) is threefold.
"Even by me was he meditated upon with the mind here as an enemy, though he is your friend;
therefore, it was through great forbearance that he has been informed of this by me in another way. That which is devoid of the measure of material substance and abandoned by reliance on results—"
One should set aside that defect of a document known as "lack of proof" (pramāṇavarjita).
One should avoid in the first stage the defect of "lack of legal title" (āgamavarjita),
as well as a case involving one person against many, or one involving opposition to a city or a kingdom.

In the case of dots (*bindu*), measures (*mātrā*), words (*pada*), and syllables (*varṇa*), if there is a single rule that is not properly observed, the text becomes deficient or excessive and thus rendered useless; one should avoid such a text with great effort. Furthermore, that which is corrupted, poorly situated, or damaged by water, oil, and the like—[is likewise to be avoided].
Even in common speech, one should avoid that which, though clear, is ambiguous in its meaning.
(NM 2.14) A statement does not constitute truth even if it is well-established, if it falls outside the bounds of established customary law. (NM 2.15; cf. Manu 8.164)
That [document] was submitted by me while he was residing on Mount Gandhamādana;
this is external to the legal procedure (*vyavahārika-dharma*) and is not established as valid.
This is because it contains the insertion of different syllables and conveys a different meaning.
The presentation of the case would be confused, and the legal procedure itself would likewise become muddled.

(NM 2.17) If, due to passion or other such motives, one party should state something contradictory during the proceedings, then all of that must first be written down by the plaintiff upon a board or similar surface. (NM 2.18)
NM2.19a/ For the sake of unconfused understanding, that which has been well-examined by those established in the Dharma [is accepted];
NM2.19c/ therefore, other things such as fruits and so forth should be excluded from the disputant's [position].
NM2.20a/ And the remainder, permitted by both disputants, remains upon the writing board.
They (the judges), along with witnesses, shall record the admissions of both litigants.

Whatever remains beyond what has been written by the two litigants, but which is subsequently remembered by a litigant, that is called the *pratyākalita*; it is recorded in its own section at the end of that case.
Whether appointed by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory or defeat belongs to those two [parties].
One who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an authorized agent [shall not litigate for another].

One who speaks for the sake of another should be punished even when speaking falsely in a legal proceeding. That man who, having abandoned his initial plea, takes up another again, should be known as one defeated by virtue of shifting his position in the debate.
In all disputes, one does not lose the case through verbal quibble (*vākchala*).
However, in matters concerning cattle, women, land, and the non-payment of debts, even if one is punished, one does not lose the substance of the claim.
If a defendant, when accused, should practice denial of the charge, [he shall be punished].
The plaintiff shall point out the matter to be proven, provided he has not been defeated by a counter-attack;
for what was written in the first part [of the plaint] must be set forth in its entirety, letter by letter,
while the claimant must establish it through evidence in the third part.

Action is also said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine. Human action is established by means of documents and witnesses; divine action is recorded as consisting of the balance-scale and other such ordeals. When a judicial proceeding is conducted during the day in villages or cities, [it is considered valid].

When witnesses are available, no divine ordeal (*divya*) should be employed as a means of proof. However, in the case of a violent crime committed in a forest, in a desolate place, at night, or inside a house,
as well as in cases of the denial of a deposit, a divine ordeal is permissible.

When the prima facie argument has been refuted by the establishment of the grounds for the opposing side, the defendant must indeed act like one who understands the prima facie case. He who, having been summoned, flees; he who remains silent; or he who is defeated by the witnesses—[is considered defeated].
And one who has admitted the claim himself; thus, the defeated party is of four kinds.

(NM 2.32) One who speaks inconsistently, one who evades the legal procedure, one who fails to appear, one who remains without a reply, and one who flees after being summoned; these are recorded as the five kinds of defeated parties. (NM 2.33)
Gems such as rubies and the like, gold such as dinars and the like,
and pearls, coral, conch shells, and so forth, when stolen, go to the owner if they are of high quality.
However, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, or even clothing, if taken without permission, [belong to the owner].

NM2.35c: Regarding the term "pādukā" (shoes/sandals), it has been stated by the King that one who steps upon it deserves death. NM2.36a: The price of merchandise, wages, a deposit, a fine, and whatever is taken in a lawsuit; NM2.36c:
A gift made in vain, stakes at dice, and gambling bets—these do not increase [with interest] unless they are intended to do so.
Those of Śūdra origin who bring false accusations against the twice-born,
the king shall have their tongues cut out and impaled upon a stake.
An edict may take the form of a written document, a scroll, or a formal decree.
Whether it be a mortgage, a sale, a purchase,
or a document, that person who first makes a formal complaint to the king should be recognized as the plaintiff by those who know the law.
When witnesses are challenged, the first step is the purification of the previous witnesses;
once those witnesses have been cleared, one should thereafter purify the testimony itself.
When witnesses, assessors, or the judge are challenged, there must be a renewed examination.
But for those who have completed their own prescribed conduct, there is no rule for returning to rebirth.
Even one who has surrendered himself, or even one who has completed his own conduct,
or even one who has failed in his ritual duties, deserves the final determination by the court assembly.
Having set aside the arguments of the parties, the determination of the case must be made by the members of the court;
for if a decision is rendered without setting them aside, there will be conflict both in this world and after death.
One who has been defeated by the court members themselves must later be punished by the king according to his own legal code.
And a document of victory (jaya-patraka) should also be granted to the victor in accordance with the facts.
This has been declared by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) as the primary gateway to legal procedure;
for when the gateway is pure, the legal proceeding itself shall be pure, and not otherwise.
Mātṛkā 3 [The Assembly]:
But the appointed person must deliver a statement that is free from partiality. 1.1c/1.2a.
A member of the court who speaks what is reasonable shall incur neither hatred nor guilt;
however, a member of the court who speaks otherwise shall incur both.
The king, moreover, should appoint righteous members of the court who have been thoroughly tested.
Those who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings like excellent oxen—
skilled in the meaning of the treatises on Dharma, of noble birth, speakers of truth,
and impartial toward both enemy and friend— should be the members of the king's court.
Dharma is known to be established upon that [the king], and the king is the root of Dharma, O Prince.
Therefore, the king should purify legal proceedings in the company of the virtuous. When legal proceedings are pure, the members of the court attain purity.

Their purification comes from dharma; therefore, one should speak only the truth regarding dharma. For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while they look on, there the members of the court are themselves slain.
For when a dharma pierced by adharma enters the court,
if it is not extracted from its wound, the members of that court are themselves pierced.
Either the court should not be entered at all, or one must speak what is correct and just.
Whether by failing to speak or by speaking falsely, a man becomes guilty of sin.
(9) But those members of the court who, having entered the assembly hall, sit silently lost in thought and do not state what has been presented before them—all of them are speakers of falsehood. (10)
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness,
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes tainted by sin, yet the members of the court are released.

The sin goes to the perpetrator when one who deserves censure is censured. He who, having entered the assembly, speaks behind someone's back due to a deficiency in his purpose, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man who is indifferent to the consequences.
Therefore, having entered the court, a member of the assembly, free from passion and hatred,
should speak such words that he does not fall into hell.
Just as a learned physician extracts a dart by means of surgical instruments and skillful technique, [so should the judge act].
Likewise, the judge should extract the thorn from the legal proceeding.
Where all the members of the court consider, "This is right," that dispute shall be free of the thorn; otherwise, it remains possessed of the thorn.
That is no assembly where there are no elders;
those are not elders who do not speak according to the Dharma;
that is not the Dharma where there is no truth.
That which is permeated by deceit is not truth. 17. Legal Subjects: 1. Non-payment of Debt.

That which is to be given and that which is not to be given, by whom, where, and in what manner, as well as the rules for giving and receiving— this is traditionally known as the law of the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*).
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares.
Whether they are divided or undivided, those who bear that burden [must pay]. Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle or a brother,
or whatever was contracted by a mother for the sake of the family, the heirs shall pay all of that in its entirety.
A debt that has been cleared by sons, which was incurred in due order and remains uncontradicted, must be paid by grandsons; it ceases with the fourth generation.
Since fathers desire sons for the sake of their own interests, [they act accordingly].

"He will liberate me from my creditors, both those to whom I owe and those who owe me. Therefore, once a son is born, the father should strive with effort to liberate himself from debt through his son, so that he does not fall into hell.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still in debt,
both his asceticism and his fire-sacrifice become the property of his creditors. A father shall not pay a son’s debt, but a son may pay a father’s debt.
Except for that contracted through lust, anger, wine, gambling, or acting as a surety;
and except for that which was contracted at the father’s own command or for the maintenance of the family;
whatever debt has been contracted in times of distress, the father shall pay that to the son. (Nārada Smṛti 1.8c–9)

Whatever has been set aside for the sake of the family by the disciples, resident pupils, slaves, wives, or those performing domestic service, that must be carried on by the head of the household. A son shall not [claim his inheritance] before twenty years have passed while his father is away abroad.

One should pay the debt to the paternal uncle or to the eldest brother. Even if he is the only one remaining, he may be made to pay a debt contracted by those authorized while they were alive. But when they have died, his son is not liable to pay that debt contracted by others.
A woman shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband, nor likewise one contracted by her son,
except for what was promised by her own consent, or what was contracted jointly with her husband. A childless widow, authorized by her dying husband, shall pay [the debt].

Or rather, he who takes the inheritance shall [pay] that debt, for the debt follows the inheritance. Furthermore, a debt contracted by a wife shall in no way become the responsibility of her husband, except for what was contracted during times of distress; for the expansion of the family’s affairs is for the sake of men.
Except for the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and vintners,
whose livelihood depends on them and whose families rely upon them;
but a woman who, having sons, abandons her son and resorts to another man [is guilty].
The son alone shall take the entire inheritance of that woman who is destitute of wealth.
But if a woman who possesses property and has offspring should resort to another man,
he shall pay her husband’s debt, or she may be abandoned by him in that same manner.
For when a man dies without wealth and without sons, he who takes his wife incurs the debt; that very person is declared by tradition to be the heir to his property.
Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the burden of the debt.
If there is neither a son nor a woman possessing property, the one who takes the woman inherits the property of both the woman and the man.

Among women who live as they please, she who is the most excellent, and among remarried women (*punarbhū*), she who is the most excellent— the one who marries such a woman shall pay the debt contracted by her husband.
They say that transactions performed by a woman are not authoritative in times of non-distress,
especially those involving the giving, mortgaging, or selling of a house or field.
Even these are valid if the husband gives his consent.

In the absence of the husband, the son [shall take it], or in the absence of both husband and son, the king. What has been given by a gratified husband to his wife, even when he has died, she may enjoy at her pleasure or give away, with the exception of immovable property.

Likewise, a deed performed by a slave is declared to be as if not done, except by the master’s command; for a slave has no authority over himself. And a deed performed by a son against the will of the father is likewise [invalid].
They say that even such a gift is as good as not given; a slave and a son are both equal in this regard.
Even if he is independent, one who has not attained legal capacity is not liable for debt.
Independence, however, is recorded as belonging to the eldest, where seniority is determined by qualities and age.

In this world, there are three independent persons: the king, the teacher, and likewise the householder in his own home for each and every member of the castes. All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth alone is independent.
A student is declared to be dependent, whereas independence resides in the teacher.
Women, sons, and slaves, along with their possessions, are dependent;
however, the householder therein is independent regarding that which has come to him by inheritance.
A child staying in the womb is to be considered equal [to his parents] until the eighth year;
he is known as a *bāla* (infant) until the sixteenth year, and is also termed a *pogaṇḍa*. Beyond that age, he is knowledgeable in legal affairs and independent, except in relation to his parents.
While both parents are alive, he shall remain dependent, even if he is advanced in age.
Of these two, the father is superior, because the importance of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, it is the mother; and in her absence, the eldest brother.
All these [sons] are always independent with respect to their own property, but they are considered dependent in all matters concerning the property of others;
they are regarded as masters only in regard to instruction, distribution, and sale.
Whatever transaction a minor performs, and likewise one who is not independent, [is invalid].
Those who know the treatises declare in the treatises that such an act is "unperformed.
For even if one who is independent performs an action while having fallen into a state of non-normality, they say that too is indeed unperformed;
he is not independent for that reason.
Those who are obsessed by lust and anger, afflicted by pain, fear, or calamity, and overwhelmed by passion and hatred, should be known as having fallen from their natural state (*aprakṛti*).
Likewise, the eldest in the family, as well as one who is preeminent and remains established in his natural state, [should be respected].
An act performed by such a person shall be considered as unperformed; what is done by one who lacks independence is not considered done.
All legal actions have wealth as their foundation; therefore, effort is required for its acquisition.
Its regulation follows this sequence: protection, increase, and enjoyment.
Furthermore, that [wealth] should be known as threefold: pure (*śukla*), variegated (*śabala*), and black (*kṛṣṇa*). Its seven distinct varieties should be understood separately:
that which is acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, a pupil, a client, or inheritance.
Wealth is of seven kinds, and "white" (śukla) wealth is one of them; its increase is likewise of that same kind.
Wealth acquired through usury, agriculture, trade, tolls, crafts, service, and what is obtained from one who has been assisted, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).
That which is acquired through gambling with dice, serving as a messenger, distress, forgery, violence,
or by means of fraud is declared to be "black" (kṛṣṇa).
By means of that [wealth], one may perform buying, selling, giving, or receiving.
And various activities as well as enjoyments proceed [from it].
Whatever a man performs with whatever kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit both hereafter and in this world.
Furthermore, that [wealth] is traditionally held to be of twelve kinds based on its relation to the respective social classes (*varṇa*):
three are common to all, while the remaining nine are traditionally held to be specific. These are:
what has come down by succession, a gift of affection, and what is acquired together with one's wife.
N1.47c: For all social classes without distinction, wealth is of three kinds.

N1.48a: The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as having three characteristics: N1.48c: that which is obtained through receiving gifts, from officiating at sacrifices, and likewise from teaching pupils.

They declare that there are also three specific types of wealth for a Kṣatriya: that acquired in battle, tribute, and fines from judicial proceedings. (49) One should know that the specific wealth of a Vaiśya likewise has three characteristics. (50a)

For a Śūdra, however, [the means of livelihood] are agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade, provided they are performed under the patronage of those [higher castes]. This is the lawful acquisition of wealth for all social classes;
it would be unlawful by way of the reverse, unless there is a grave emergency.
In times of distress, the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa is ordained to be that which is next in order;
thereafter, the conduct of a Vaiśya is prescribed, but never that which is lower. A Brāhmaṇa should by no means perform the work of a Śūdra.
A Śūdra is not entitled to perform Vedic rites, for those two [the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya] are subject to the loss of caste by performing them.
Between those two, neither a superior nor an inferior occupation exists;
having set aside the middle occupations, the other duties are common to all.
Having crossed over a time of distress by means of wealth acquired through the occupation of a Kṣatriya,
a Brāhmaṇa should abandon that Kṣatriya occupation after performing purification for himself. However, if a Brāhmaṇa takes delight out of passion in that very occupation, [he must perform penance].
A *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* who has fallen from the path is proclaimed to be unworthy of the company at a meal.
Regarding the livelihood of a Vaiśya, there are certain things that must not be sold by a Brāhmaṇa: milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, beeswax, lac, alkali, juice, and fermented liquor.
Meat, cooked rice, sesame, linen, soma, flowers, fruits, vegetables,
humans, poison, weapons, water, salt, cakes, and climbing plants;
indigo, silk, skins, bones, blankets made of hair, one-hoofed animals, and earth.
Curdled milk, hair, oil-cakes, vegetables, and similar medicinal herbs [are forbidden for sale].
However, dry wood and grass may be sold by a Brāhmaṇa,
with the exception of fragrant substances, lac, bamboo, cotton, roots, and chaff.
Split bamboo that has fallen of its own accord, fruits of the *badara* and *iṅguda* trees,
a rope, and cotton thread— provided these have not been altered;
likewise, in cases of inability, for the sake of medicine, or for the purpose of a sacrifice.

If sesame seeds must necessarily be sold, they should be exchanged for an equal amount of grain. A Brāhmaṇa who sells items that ought not to be sold falls away from the path; having been restored to the right path, he shall be punished severely by the king.
The means of proof must be diligently protected by those who abide by the law of proof;
for the means of proof fail when they are not properly established by the authorities.
Written documents, witnesses, and possession are recorded as the threefold means of proof.
In the acquisition of wealth, that by which the owner enjoys his property [is decisive].
A written document is always superior; witnesses, however, are effective only while they live.
Through the lapse of time, possession prevails—this is the settled rule in the scriptures. (Nārada Smṛti 1.65c–66)

Among these three types of visible evidence, each preceding one should be known as more authoritative than the following; possession is the most authoritative of them all. Indeed, even when a written document exists and witnesses are still living, [possession prevails].
Especially in the case of immovable property, that which is not enjoyed does not remain secure.
When a person, out of folly, neglects his own property while it is being enjoyed by others even in his presence,
possession brings those things under its control despite him being alive.
Whatever property a wealth-owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years in his presence,
while remaining silent, he does not deserve to recover it.
For him who remains standing by, indifferent and silent, [the property is lost].
If the previously mentioned time limit has elapsed, the legal suit is not successful.
However, if the owner is neither mentally incapacitated nor a minor, and his property is enjoyed by another, that enjoyment constitutes a valid legal claim; the possessor deserves that wealth.

A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, the property of the king, and the property of a Vedic scholar are not lost through adverse possession (upabhoga). Furthermore,
even in the case of actual enjoyment by the owner, [the property is not lost] for twenty years.
Even mortgages and the like are lost through adverse possession, with the exception of the property of a woman or a king;
however, the property of a woman and that of kings is never lost,
even after being enjoyed for hundreds of years without a legal title.

Where possession is seen but no title is seen anywhere, there title is the cause, not possession; there, possession is not the cause. That which is enjoyed without title—possession does not override that.

But when the enjoyer has died, the property passes to the state of being enjoyed by his descendants. One who seizes [property] should, when challenged, produce evidence for the objects; possession alone shall be the proof of purity for those acquired from one's father in due succession.
That which is deposited with another, that which is taken away, that which is left behind, that which is seized by force, that which is borrowed,
and that which is enjoyed in the owner's absence— these six [types of property] are lost without legal title (āgama).
Likewise, when a litigant has passed away while a lawsuit was pending, [the case continues].
That property must be cleared up by the son; possession does not override it.
(80) If something has been enjoyed for three generations by predecessors even without a title, that cannot be overturned, having come down through the succession of three persons. (81)
Even if they are virtuous, witnesses are not authoritative after the wealth-owner has died,
except for what was previously communicated by the one who was himself on the verge of death.
For when the defendant is dead, the testimony of witnesses is not considered valid evidence.
In that case, a proceeding accompanied by witnesses shall be the means of proof for reaching a definitive decision.

(83) Furthermore, even if he is ill, one who has been made to hear a matter connected with dharma may serve as a witness there even after death; this applies also in the case of the six types of transactions, such as deposits and the like. (84)
In all matters concerning debts and the like, each subsequent [means of proof] is stronger than the preceding one;
however, among those acquired through gift or purchase, each preceding one is more authoritative.
For the giving and receiving of gifts is intended for the purpose of securing a specific status or acquisition.
That is declared to be *kusīda* (lending on interest), and by that means the livelihood of money-lenders (*kusīdinaḥ*) is sustained.
In the treatises, its interest is recorded as being of four kinds: corporeal (*kāyikā*), periodical (*kālikā*), stipulated (*kāritā*), and compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
That which is not inconsistent with one's physical state and is paid as wages for manual labor is known as bodily interest (*kāyikā*).
That interest which flows month by month is remembered as periodical interest (*kālikā*).
That interest which is made by the debtor himself is called stipulated interest (*kāritā*).
Interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*.
This rule for generating interest is known as the universal standard for debts;
however, there is another rule according to local custom where the debt remains outstanding.
In one place it is double, in another triple, and likewise in another it is fourfold;
in yet another region, it remains eightfold.
The interest on gold, grain, and cloth is respectively double, triple, and fourfold.
The interest on ghee is eightfold; likewise, the offspring of female cattle and other animals [constitutes the interest].
[Interest is also paid] on thread, cotton, fermenting agents, tin, lead, all types of weapons, leather, copper, and iron.
And for all other kinds of bricks as well,
Prajāpati Manu has declared that their increase is inexhaustible;
this applies likewise to all oils, intoxicating liquors, honey, and clarified butter.
The interest on molasses and salt should be known to be eightfold.
There shall never be interest on gifts made out of affection that were not requested;
yet even such an unrequested gift increases after half a year has passed.
This rule for interest has been declared according to dharma for one who has grown wealthy. However, that which is prescribed as interest on grain is termed usury (vārdhuṣya).
A Vaiśya may, at his will, overcome distress through the practice of usury.

Even in the midst of dire calamities, a Brāhmaṇa must not engage in usury. If a Brāhmaṇa who has heirs is unable to repay what is owed to him, one should pay it to a member of his own family; in his absence, to his kinsmen.

But when there are no kinsmen of his own, nor relatives or friends, then he should give [the debt] to those of his own caste; if none of these exist, he should cast it into the water. Having received a debtor who has come to him, the creditor shall pay the amount due to that debtor.
But if, when being requested, he does not give, he shall incur the loss of his remaining property.
When the debt is cleared, he should provide a written discharge; in the absence of such a document, he should provide a verbal acknowledgment.
In this manner, there shall be mutual clearance between the creditor and the debtor.
In this matter, there are two causes for confidence: the guarantor (*pratibhū*) and the pledge (*ādhi*). Written evidence and witnesses are the two means of proof that bring about clarity.
Likewise, they serve for appearance, for delivery, and for assurance.
The wise have observed that a surety is of three kinds, pertaining to exactly three matters.
When debtors fail to repay their debts, or when the terms of repayment are disputed,
the guarantor shall pay that debt, as shall one who fails to produce the debtor.
If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to the agreement;
for when no specific distinction has been made among them, the creditor may act as he pleases.
Whatever amount a surety may pay when pressured by the creditor, the debtor shall reimburse that amount to the surety doubled.
That which is made subject [to another's control] is known as *ādhi* (pledge); it should be understood as being of two kinds.

A pledge is of two kinds: that for which a specific time has been fixed, and that which is to be surrendered as soon as the debt is ready to be paid. Furthermore, it is said to be of two types: one to be kept (gopya) and likewise one to be used (bhogya).
In the case of the former, there is a return of the object; in the opposite case (the latter), there is a loss of interest.
Likewise, if through negligence the pledge of a wealthy man undergoes deterioration or is destroyed—
unless caused by acts of God or the king— the principal shall be lost. Even if it is being guarded, if the pledge should become worthless over time, [the same applies].
Another pledge may be provided, or the debt must be paid to the creditor.
Now, if a debtor should become deprived of his means due to a change in circumstances,

he should be made to pay the debt as it becomes possible for him to do so, at each appropriate time, according to his income. Or, if a capable debtor, out of malice, does not pay the wealth to the creditor, [he shall be compelled to pay].
The king, having taken a twentieth part as his share, should cause [the debt] to be paid.
If the debtor's debt amount should be lost here over time, it is traditionally held that the recovery of caste, name, and residence may be established through a document.
A document is to be known as being of two kinds: that written in one's own hand and that written by another.
Whether a matter lacks witnesses or possesses witnesses, its proof depends on the established customs of the region.
A document that is not contrary to local customs, which clearly indicates the subject matter and the parties involved, and whose sequence and letters are uncorrupted, is recognized as valid evidence.
That which is done under the duress of a drunkard, a creditor, a woman, or a child;
likewise, that which is done by one who is frightened or through fraud;
and where the witnesses, the creditor, the debtor, and the scribe have died—[such transactions] are rendered invalid.
Even that which is written is rendered useless, except in the case of a mortgage (ādhi) which has a stable basis.
119. It has been stated that a pledge (ādhi) is of two kinds: movable and immovable;
in this case, the validity of both depends upon possession, and not otherwise. 120.
That which was shown at the proper time, and that which was proclaimed or caused to be proclaimed [in the presence of witnesses].
A written document is established as valid everywhere, even when the witnesses have died. However,
a document that has not been heard of, one whose meaning is not seen, or one that exists solely for the purpose of litigation does not attain validity,
even while the witnesses are still living.
When a document has been deposited in another country, burnt, poorly written, or stolen, there shall be a determination of its validity based on the time;
for one who possesses it, by means of a timely procedure, and for one who does not possess it, by means of the examination of witnesses.
In any case where there may be doubt regarding a document—whether it was produced or not produced—[the truth must be determined].
One should validate it by means of the signature of the party's own hand, possession, and logical consistency.
A document that bears another person's name or was produced for some other purpose must be examined when there is a dispute, by means of the reasons of connection and provenance.
Any document that bears another's name or has been produced for some other purpose must,
in case of dispute, be examined by means of connections, traditional accounts, and reasons.

A written document may be contested by means of another written document; a document with witnesses may be contested by witnesses. A document is superior to witnesses, but witnesses are superior to a document.
[This applies] in cases where the document is torn, broken, stolen, wiped out, lost, or poorly written.
Another document must be executed; this is remembered as the rule for documents.
But when matters are in doubt between two parties disputing,
the clarification of the truth is obtained from witnesses, because they have seen, heard, or experienced [the events].
A witness is to be understood as one who has seen or heard with his ears and eyes:
that which another says is for the ear, and that which is bodily action is for the eye.
Wise men have observed that there are eleven kinds of witnesses;
among them, five are said to be appointed and six are unappointed. These are:
the written witness, the reminded witness, and the incidental witness.
The secret witness and the corroborating witness: thus the witness is declared to be of five kinds.
The unestablished [verdict] is also proclaimed by the wise to be of six kinds:
that of the village, that of the judge, and that of the king for those engaged in legal proceedings.
Those who are insiders in legal matters, those sent by the plaintiff, and family members in disputes between families— these too may serve as witnesses.
Worthy witnesses should be of noble birth, upright, pure by birth, action, and wealth; they should be at least three in number, irreproachable, pure, and possessed of sound intellect.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those who are blameless— these may belong to each respective caste, or alternatively, all may belong to all castes.
In guilds, the members of the guild; in their respective groups, those belonging to the group; among outsiders, the outsiders; and among women, women themselves shall be witnesses.
But if someone within groups such as guilds should become an object of hatred, he shall not be a witness for those very same people; they are all his haters.
For even those who are not witnesses are seen in the treatises to be of five kinds by the wise:
[those who testify] from verbal command, from defect, from division, from their own admission, and those who die in the interval.

Where there are witnesses in a legal dispute, a disagreement may arise due to differences: some being learned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) and so forth based on their testimony, while others being thieves and so forth based on the observation of their faults.
One who, not previously designated by his own statement, comes of his own accord and speaks;
or one who dies in the interval after the claimant has passed away, except for the case where he had been informed while on the verge of death.
Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those men who have renounced the world are not witnesses; this is by their own declaration, and no further reason is stated here.
Thieves, violent assailants, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise murderers—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; truth is not found in them.
When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter,
those whose testimony differs shall be considered non-witnesses because of that discrepancy.
But he who, not being appointed as a witness, comes of his own accord and speaks, is called a "sūcī" (informant) in the legal treatises; he does not deserve the status of a witness.
If the matter that ought to be made known does not exist, or if there is no claimant, where could he exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness.
If the matter that ought to be made known does not exist, or if there is no claimant, where could he exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness.
When two parties are disputing over a matter and there are witnesses for both,
those who are witnesses for the one whose case is the first to be presented shall be the witnesses.
In whatever matter the weakness of the plaintiff's case arises due to his own conduct,
the witnesses in that dispute must be questioned by the defendant.
One should not approach a witness in private who has been directed by another;
nor should one cause him to be divided from others by means of another person; acting in this manner, one shall certainly suffer defeat.
If a witness designated for testimony should die or depart to another region, those who heard it shall be the authority; for the subsequent action depends upon the evidence.
Even after a very long period of time, a written document attains validity;
one who knows how to write should write it himself, but one who does not know should have it written by another.
The validity of a witness who has been reminded here is stated to be established after the eighth year;
likewise, the validity of one who appears by chance is established up to the fifth year.
Success for a secret witness is attained until the third year;
they say that success for a subsequent witness is achieved until the end of the year.
Alternatively, no fixed time limit has been observed regarding witnesses;
for those learned in the scriptures say that witnesshood depends upon memory.
That man whose memory and hearing are never impaired,
even over a very long period of time, is fit to serve as a witness to a legal matter.
But other six types of disputes are declared to be those where there is no reliance on witnesses;
the wise say that for these, the very characteristics [of the case] constitute witness-status.
One who sets fire with a torch in hand is to be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer;
and one seized by the hair of his head is a simultaneous adulterer.
One with a spade in hand should be known as a destroyer of embankments when found nearby;
likewise, one with an axe in hand is proclaimed to be a cutter of forest trees.
A man who commits assault is to be recognized by his prominent physical marks;
for these cases of assault are not dependent on witnesses, but rather require an investigation of the facts.
Someone, having marked himself, might out of malice cause harm to another;
in such a case, an investigation is appropriate by means of the evidence, the purpose, the circumstances, and the capability.
Those who have a financial interest in the matter, those who are not trustworthy, those who are associates, those who are enemies,
those whose faults are known, those afflicted by disease, and those who are corrupted should not be questioned as witnesses.
Slaves, rogues, the faithless, the elderly, women, children, and wheelwrights; those who are intoxicated, insane, negligent, afflicted, gamblers, and village priests.
Long-distance travelers, sea-faring merchants, renunciants, and the sick;
hunters, Vedic scholars, those who have abandoned proper conduct, eunuchs, and actors.

Atheists, those who have not undergone the *vrātya* initiation, those who have abandoned their wives or the sacred fires, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, those who eat from a single vessel, companions of enemies, those who live by trade, and kinsmen of the same lineage.

Actors whose faults have been previously observed, poison-sellers, snake-charmers, those who administer poison, arsonists, debtors, the sons of Śūdra women, those born of illicit unions, the exhausted, the reckless, the weary, the penniless, and outcasts; N1.164a:
the indigent, the violent, the fatigued, the destitute, and those of the lowest castes.
Those who have broken their conduct, those who have not returned from their studies, the dull-witted, oil-pressers, and root-diggers; N1.164c.

Those possessed by spirits, those who hate the king, those who predict rain or the positions of the stars, those who proclaim evil omens, those who sell themselves, and those who live by the service of the genitals— these are excluded.

One with deformed nails, one with a dark-complexioned face, one afflicted with vitiligo, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, a vintner, a magician, a hunter, a fierce man, and those who oppose guilds or corporations; N1.166.
A murderer, a painter, a dancer, one who has fallen from his caste,
a forger, a cheat, one who has renounced [his vows], a thief, and a king’s servant;
[as well as those who deal in] human beings, poison, weapons, water, salt, cakes, and climbing plants.
The seller, the Brāhmaṇa, the twice-born usurer, and he who [is such].
One who has fallen from his own duty, a member of a guild, a panegyrist, a servant of the low, one disputing with his father, and a creator of dissension— these are non-witnesses.
Those who have been designated as non-witnesses— such as slaves, dishonest persons, and others—
may also become witnesses when the gravity of the matter requires it.
In all cases of violence, in theft and adultery,
and in both forms of verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely.
Among them, neither a child, nor one who is alone, nor a woman, nor a forger,
nor a kinsman, nor an enemy shall give false testimony.
A child may speak falsely through ignorance, a woman through wicked habit, a forger out of malice,
a kinsman out of affection, and an enemy out of a desire for revenge.
Alternatively, if a person is agreed upon by two parties who are disputing,
even if he is alone, he may be questioned as a witness in the assembly.
But he who, because he is broken by his own faults, appears as if unwell,
moves from place to place and approaches each one individually.
He coughs restlessly and unexpectedly, sighs repeatedly,
scratches the ground with his feet, and tosses his arms or his garment.
The color of his face changes, and likewise his forehead perspires;
his lips become parched, and he looks upward and sideways.
He who speaks much at random, as if in haste, even when unasked, should be known as a false witness; the king shall punish that sinner.
And he who, having caused others to hear [the testimony], then denies his status as a witness,
must be punished even more severely, for he is worse than a false witness.
Having summoned the witnesses— who are known for their conduct and who understand the facts of the case— he should question them individually after binding them with solemn oaths.
One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all the mortal sins.
Having thoroughly intimidated the witnesses by means of ancient declarations of dharma, by proclaiming the greatness of truth, and by censuring falsehood.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a begging bowl, tormented by hunger and thirst, and wretched,
he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar.
He who would give false testimony might find himself besieged within a city, starving at its outer gate, and beholding his enemies once again.

The night on which a woman is taken as a wife, the night on which one is defeated at dice, and the night on which one's limbs are tormented by a heavy burden— on those nights, the speaker of falsehood shall dwell.
A witness who, when summoned to testify, behaves with the laxity of an ox's ear,
fastens upon himself a thousand nooses of Varuṇa.
When a hundred years of that [time] are completed, he is released from one noose;
in this manner, he is liberated from that bondage after a million years.
Listen, gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he destroys by speaking falsely in testimony, in that specific case, according to the sequence of their enumeration.
One kills five by lying about cattle, one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and one kills a thousand by lying about men.
By speaking falsehood for the sake of gold, one destroys both those born and those unborn;
by falsehood regarding land, one destroys everything. Therefore, do not speak falsehood regarding land.
They say that truth alone is the unique, peerless purifier of the self; it is the ladder to heaven, like a boat for crossing from this shore to the other.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices.
A single well is better than a hundred wells, and a single large pond is better than a hundred ponds;
a single sacrifice is better than a hundred sacrifices, and truth is better than a hundred sons.
The earth supports [all beings] by truth; by truth the sun rises;
by truth the wind blows; and by truth the waters flow.
Truth alone is the supreme gift; truth alone is the supreme austerity;
truth alone is the highest dharma for the worlds—thus have we heard.
In brief, O gods, truth is the characteristic of humans, while falsehood is traditionally held to be their nature;
yet he whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
Speak the truth, abandoning falsehood; by the truth you shall go to heaven.
Having spoken a most terrible falsehood, one will fall into hell.
And in the hells, those fierce and powerful servants of Yama will constantly cut out their tongues and sever them with swords.
And, unprovoked by anger, they shall pierce with spears the wailing man who has no refuge;
and having lifted him up with his head downward, they shall hurl him into lakes of fire.
Having experienced those long-lasting sufferings of hell,
you shall go here, O unfortunate one, into the wombs of vultures, crows, and other such creatures.
Having understood these faults in falsehood and having understood the excellent qualities in truth, speak the truth and uplift yourself; do not cause yourself to fall.
Neither kinsmen, nor friends, nor even great riches are able to rescue one who is sinking into the terrible darkness.
But the ancestors hang on you now that you have become their witness:
"Will he deliver us, or will he cause himself to fall?"
Truth is the self of man; everything is established upon truth. In every way, you shall unite yourself with the self through that which is beneficial.
The interval between the night you were born and the night you will die would be in vain for you, if you were to act otherwise than truthfully.
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood;
therefore, especially in the matter of witness-dharma, one should speak only the truth.
That lowest of men who employs his own speech for the sake of another—
what evil would that sinner not do for his own sake, being fearless of hell?
Meanings are indeed fixed in speech; they have their root in speech and have issued forth from speech.
For that man who would steal this speech is a thief of everything.
But in the event of a conflict among witnesses, the majority is the authority;
if they are equal in number, those who are pure should be accepted; if they are equal in purity, those with the better memory should be accepted.
But where, in a legal dispute, an equality of witness accounts is observed due to the presence of those with good memories,
the testimony is set aside again because of the subtle nature of the requirements for a witness.
When the categories of facts have been specified, if a witness, having come to give testimony,
does not speak in accordance with the syllables [of the deposition], that shall not be considered properly stated.
Where there is a contradiction regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, or caste,
that testimony is said to be invalid.
Where witnesses state a matter either less than or more than it actually is, that too shall be considered as unstated; this is recorded as the rule for witnesses.
Where, due to negligence, there is neither a document nor witnesses for a creditor,
and the plaintiff denies the debt, the threefold procedure prescribed therein [shall apply].
An injunction appropriate to the time, a fragment of reasoning, and likewise a third means—oath—has been declared; by these one should establish [the truth] in due order.
If one who is being repeatedly exhorted should reject those words,
then after three, four, or five times, he shall bring about that matter for him.
But when there is an obstruction to the injunction, one should pursue it through fragments of reasoning by means of place,
time, purpose, connection, quantity, action, and so forth.
Even when arguments are insufficient, one should distress him with oaths,
taking into account the nature of the matter, the time, and the strength of the case, by means of fire, water, good deeds, and so forth.
He whom a blazing fire does not burn, and whom water holds back, escapes the curse; in the opposite case, he becomes a sinner.
In cases where women are accused of violating their moral conduct, as well as in cases of theft or violence,
and likewise in all instances of denial of facts, this same rule is prescribed.
For even oaths among the gods and the sages are recorded;
Vasiṣṭha, being suspicious of a sorcerer, pronounced an oath.
Likewise, the Seven Sages, having assembled at Puṣkara for the sake of Indra,
uttered a solemn oath with undistracted minds for the sake of mutual purification.
If one who has committed an improper act of violence seeks to make amends,
or if he himself confesses it in the assembly, half of the prescribed fine is ordained for him.
But if, out of wickedness, he conceals his sin, he shall be defeated;
in such a case, the members of the court are not satisfied, and a severe punishment is inflicted.
2. Deposit (*nikṣepa*):
Where one deposits one's own property out of trust, without hesitation, that is called "deposit" by the wise as a title of legal dispute.
When an object that is separated from other substances and is indeterminate in nature is deposited in another's house, that is known as *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit).
Furthermore, that [loan] is declared to be of two kinds: with witnesses and otherwise;
likewise, in the case of the opposite, the means of proof shall be the repayment of the object itself.
But he who, being requested by the depositor, does not hand over the deposit, shall be fined by the king and compelled to pay it; and if it has been lost, he shall be made to pay its equivalent.
And he who should recover the property without the permission of the depositor shall be punished for that act and shall restore it together with interest.
If that which was lost together with the object of the deposit is destroyed, it is lost to the depositor;
the same applies if it is destroyed by an act of God or the king, provided it was not caused by his own dishonesty.
This same rule is seen to apply in the cases of borrowed items, articles held for safekeeping, and so forth;
as well as in the case of artisans, deposits, pledges, and counter-pledges.
And that man who adopts a minor (pogaṇḍa) together with his property—for him also this same rule shall apply;
these six procedures are equal.
3. Partnership (Saṃbhūyasamutthāna). Where merchants and others perform work collectively, that is known as partnership, a head of legal dispute (vyavahārapada).

When those who, for the sake of the fruit, perform their work together by means of an expedient, the deposit serves as their common basis; therefore, they may recover it according to their respective shares.
Whether equal, superior, or inferior, whatever the proportion of a person may be,
their loss, expenditure, and increase shall likewise be of that same kind.
Established in their own agreement, they shall, without deviation, supervise the merchandise, the bundles, the expenses, the profits, the loads, and the quality.
He who has lost [the goods] through negligence, as well as he who has done what was forbidden,
and he who acts without being instructed by all the partners acting in concert, shall be made to pay [the loss].
When a calamity arising from gods, thieves, or the king has occurred,
he who protects that [property] by his own power is declared to be entitled to a tenth share.
If one of them should meet with misfortune, his heir shall receive that property;
or, if there is no heir, all [the brothers] together, provided they are capable, shall take it.

N3.08a. Likewise, in the event of a calamity befalling the officiating priests, another person may complete that ritual act. N3.08c. He shall receive the allotted share of the sacrificial fee from that [original patron].
If a priest abandons a patron who is blameless and has done him no wrong,
or if a patron abandons a blameless priest, both of them shall be punished.
The officiating priest (ṛtvij) is seen to be of three kinds: one previously engaged, one chosen by oneself, and one who performs the priestly office out of affection and of his own accord.
This rule applies to those who have come by succession and to officiating priests chosen by oneself;
however, in the case of a priest engaged by chance, there is no sin in relinquishing him.
A merchant arriving at a customs station shall pay the duty as it is established;
he must not evade it, for this is ordained as a tribute to kings.
One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
or one who declares a false quantity, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.
If a certain merchant, while traveling from his country, should die as a guest,
the king shall protect his merchandise until his heirs appear.
If there is no heir, one should hand over that property to the relatives or the kinsmen;
in their absence, one should keep it well-guarded for ten years.
After ten years, property that has no owner and no heir shall be taken by the king for himself; in this way, the law is not violated.
4.d. Non-delivery of what has been given (Dattāpradānika):
When one, having given property improperly, desires to take it back, that is recorded in law as the legal dispute known as non-delivery of what has been given.
That which is not to be given, that which is to be given, that which has been given, and that which has not been given:
in legal proceedings, the path of giving is to be understood as fourfold.
For in that regard, eight things are traditionally held to be non-givable, and the givable is said to be of one kind;
one should know that what has been given is of seven kinds, and what has not been given consists of sixteen types.
A loan for use, a borrowed item, a pledge, that which is held in common,
a deposit, one's wife and children, and one's entire property [may not be sold] when there is a descendant.
For even when a living being is situated in the midst of dire calamities, the teachers have declared that certain things must not be given: namely, that which has already been promised to another.
Whatever wealth remains in excess after supporting one's family must be given away;
if one gives something other than that, one incurs guilt.

Those who know the law of giving recognize as a gift that which is given for the price of merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, from affection, in return for a favor, or for the purpose of a woman’s dowry or as a mark of favor.
But what is taken without it being given may be so through the force of fear, anger, grief, or disease;
likewise, through bribery, jesting, a reversal of roles, or the employment of trickery.

That which is performed by one who is a child, deluded, not independent, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane; and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my agent" (i.e., he will perform this work for me).
If one says "this is a worthy recipient" when he is not, or if an act is performed that is joined with unrighteousness,
whatever is given through such ignorance is declared by tradition to be as if not given at all.
He who, out of greed, takes what is not given, and he who gives what should not be given,
are both to be punished— the thief of what was not given and the giver of what should not be given.
5. Non-fulfillment of Service (Abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā): But he who, having undertaken service, does not perform it—this legal head of dispute is called "non-fulfillment of service after undertaking."
In the treatise, the wise have observed five types of attendants;
four types are laborers, and among them, the slaves are fifteen-fold.
Pupils, resident students, and hired servants—the fourth being the laborer for extra work—these are declared to be "laborers" (karmakara); slaves, however, are those born in the house and so forth.

The wise have declared that their lack of independence is their common characteristic; however, the distinction between them, as well as their specific occupations, is said to be determined by their birth and their actions.
Action also should be known as being of two kinds: indeed, the inauspicious and the auspicious.
The inauspicious is said to be the work of a slave; the auspicious is recorded as the work of those who perform [right] action.
The cleaning of house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; the touching of private parts, the handling of food remnants, and the removal of feces and urine.
Service performed at the master's will with one's own limbs, or even with the utmost devotion, should be understood as inauspicious work; that which is other than this is auspicious.
Until he has mastered the sciences, the student should serve his teacher with self-restraint;
he should likewise adopt the same conduct toward the teacher’s wives and the teacher’s son.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should wander for alms, sleep on the ground, remain unadorned,
go to bed last of all, and rise before everyone else in the house of his teacher.
One should not go anywhere without being instructed, nor should one remain with the teacher unless so directed;
when instructed, however, one should perform the task if capable, without hesitation.
He should study at the proper time as long as the teacher is not mentally distressed;
he should sit below the teacher on a grass mat or a wooden plank, with a concentrated mind.
If a pupil, though instructed by his teacher, does not follow his directions,
the teacher may punish him without causing physical injury, using either a rope or a split bamboo cane.
One should not strike him excessively, nor on the head or the chest;
having first instructed and gained his confidence, he may then be punished by the king, otherwise like a teacher.
Having returned from his studies and having presented the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) to the guru, he should return to his own home; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.
Desiring to practice his own craft, with the permission of his kinsmen,
he shall live in the presence of a teacher for a well-determined period of time.
The teacher should provide him with food from his own house and instruct him;
he should not make him perform other work, and he should treat him like a son.
He who abandons a teacher who is instructing him and is not at fault should be compelled to stay by force; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment.
Even if he has been trained, the apprentice shall receive his fee once the stipulated time has elapsed;
furthermore, whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs solely to the teacher.
Having mastered the craft within the agreed period and having circumambulated his teacher from left to right, the apprentice, after honoring him according to his ability, may depart.
A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Their wages, based on the work performed, should correspond to their ability and devotion.
In this regard, the highest wage-earner is the soldier, the middling is the farmer, and the lowest is the porter; thus is the hired laborer of three kinds.
He who is authorized over matters concerning the household is to be known as an *adhikarmakara*; he is also remembered as a *kauṭumbika*.
These four are declared to be performers of auspicious deeds;
however, the remaining fifteen types of slaves are partakers of lowly occupations.
One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an heir,
one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one who has been placed [with him] by his master.
Rescued from great debt, won as a prize in battle,
approached saying "I am yours," and made one who has completed his period of exile— these are the types of slaves.
One who becomes a slave for food, as well as one supported by a female slave,
and one who sells himself— these are recorded in the treatise as the fifteen kinds of slaves.
Among those, the first four categories are not released from servitude except by the favor of their master; for them, slavery is hereditary.
And whoever among these should rescue his master from a life-threatening danger shall be released from slavery and shall receive a share equal to that of a son.
One who was maintained during a time of famine is released from slavery by giving a pair of cattle;
however, that which was consumed during a famine cannot be purified by such an act.
Even if one has pledged the property after receiving payment, if the owner should redeem it,
then he who restores it is next in rank to the purchaser.
But by paying back the debt along with interest, the debtor is released from slavery;
even one who was made a slave by agreement is released upon the fulfillment of the stipulated time.
One who has approached saying "I am yours," having entered into battle and been won at the stake,
is released by the giving of a counter-head through an equal act.
A man who has fallen from the religious life shall indeed become the slave of the king; for him there is no release, nor is there any purification by any means whatsoever.
By neglecting his food, a *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food) is immediately released;
and by the punishment of a mare, a *vaḍavābhṛta* (slave for a mare) is released.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—
he is the most wretched of them all and is never released from slavery.
Those who have been stolen by thieves and sold, or those who have been forcibly made slaves, must be released by the king; servitude is not permitted for them.
Slavery is not ordained for the castes by means of inverse order (prātilomya);
except in the case of one who has abandoned his own duty, slavery is considered to be like marriage.
And he who, being dependent, offers himself [into slavery] saying, "I am yours," shall not obtain his desire; the former master shall regain him.
N5.39ab. Only three are declared to be without property: the wife, the slave, and likewise the son.
N5.39cd. Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
If one, with a joyful mind, should wish to make his own slave a non-slave,
he should take a water-pot from that person's shoulder and smash it along with its water.
One should strew unbroken grains together with flowers upon his head;
having said three times, "He is not a slave," one should then release him while facing eastward.
From that time forward, he should be addressed as one protected by the favor of his master;
his food may be eaten, he is worthy of receiving gifts, and he becomes beloved.
6. Non-payment of Wages (Vetanasyānapākarma). The procedure for the giving and receiving of wages for those who have been hired has been declared;
the non-payment of such wages is recorded as that title of dispute.
The master of the work shall pay wages to the hired laborer according to the sequence established for the task—
whether at the beginning, in the middle, or at the conclusion— as has been determined.
But when the wages are not fixed, the merchant, the cowherd, and the farmer shall receive a tenth part of the profit,
the cattle, the seed, and the crop, respectively.
Whatever implements for work have been brought by these [servants] for the sake of a task, he should employ them with a sense of trustworthiness; he should not act with deceit.
If one who has promised to perform work does not do so, he should be compelled by force to do it after having paid his wages;
if, having received wages, he fails to work, he shall pay double the wages.
If he should abandon his work before the time is complete, he deserves the loss of his wages;
however, if he departs due to a fault of the master, he shall receive payment for as much as he has completed.
Having agreed upon a wage consisting of a sixth part of the load, he who abandons a beast of burden on the road,
or one who does not pay after having made it work, must likewise pay the wage along with interest.
