If one hires a carrier for goods or vehicles but abandons them before reaching the destination, he shall be made to pay a fourth part of the wages; if he abandons them halfway, he shall pay half.
Likewise, a carrier who fails to convey [the goods] shall suffer a loss of wages;
however, one who causes an obstruction to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages.
If the goods should meet with disaster due to the fault of the carrier,
he shall be made to pay for whatever has been lost therein, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the fee; from two hundred, a milch cow.
This payment to the cowherd shall be made every year, along with the milk produced on the eighth day.
"O cowherd, you must bring back the cows every day at the end of the night;
having grazed and drunk, those cows the cowherd shall bring back in the evening."
If a disaster should befall the cattle, the cowherd shall strive to remedy it to the best of his ability;
if he is unable, he must quickly return and report the matter to his master.
If a herdsman fails to exert himself, raises a cry of distress, or does not inform his master,
he must bear the cost of the loss and pay a fine to the king.
If the cow is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies in a dangerous place,
or if it has failed through human negligence, the herdsman alone shall forfeit it.
Likewise, when goats and sheep are obstructed by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
if a wolf should forcibly kill one, the guilt for that shall fall upon the herdsman.
And while those cows are still unweaned and roaming together in the forest,
if a wolf should spring upon and kill one of them, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
But if cattle are stolen by thieves after having been publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his own master at the proper place and time.
By this, the dispute concerning all types of guardians has been fully explained;
and in the case of those who have died, the guardian shall be cleared of suspicion upon the discovery of the marks and other identifying signs.

Having received the fee, if a courtesan does not wish [to perform her service], she shall pay that same amount twice; if a man, having enjoyed the woman, does not pay the fee, he shall likewise pay it twice.
He who approaches a woman in a place other than the womb, or causes her to dwell with many men,
shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine.
If one has built a house within the courtyard and dwells there after paying the fee,
he should take away that house— its grass, wood, bricks, and so forth— and depart.
One should present the vessels for the hymns when they are full and at the proper time;
otherwise, what is broken or lost shall be the responsibility of the receiver, except in the case of an accident.
7. Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner (Asvāmivikraya):
When property belonging to another—whether it has been deposited, lost, found, or stolen—is sold in the absence of the owner, that should be known as sale by one who is not the owner.
Having recovered property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall take possession of it;
the buyer is cleared of guilt if the purchase was made openly, whereas theft is established if the purchase was made in secret.
One who purchases a slave from one who is not the owner, or from a person of unknown status, in secret, for a low price, or at an improper time, shall be liable for that fault.
A buyer shall not conceal the source of his purchase; his purification comes from that disclosure of the source.
In the opposite case, he incurs an equal fault and deserves the punishment for theft.
The seller shall pay the value to the owner, and the buyer shall pay the price and whatever expenses were incurred;
likewise, he shall pay a fine to the king—such is the rule regarding sale without ownership.
Having found a treasure deposited by another, one should present it to the king;
for all treasure belongs to the king, with the exception of that which belongs to Brāhmaṇas.
Even a Brāhmaṇa, having found a treasure-trove, should promptly inform the king;
he may enjoy what is given by the king, for by not reporting it, he would be a thief.
Having recovered even his own lost property in that manner, he should report it to the king;
he may take possession of it as being pure, otherwise it would be considered impure.

8. Rescission of Purchase (Krītānuśaya): When, after having sold a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the purchaser, that is called the legal subject matter known as "non-delivery after sale" (vikrīyāsaṃpradāna).
In this world, there are two kinds of property: the movable and likewise the immovable;
all of that is called "merchandise" (paṇya) in the context of the laws of purchase and sale.
N8.3a. However, the wise have recorded its method of giving and taking as being sixfold:
N8.3c. [Namely,] by counting, by weighing, by measuring, by action, by form, and by beauty.
If, after having sold a commodity for its price, one does not deliver it to the buyer,
he shall be made to pay the loss of value for immovable property, and the fruit of the labor for movable property.
If the market price should fall, he shall bring back the merchandise with its profit;
this rule applies to those who stay [in one place], while for those who travel in various directions, the profit is determined by the region.
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen,
that loss shall belong to the seller alone, since he sold it without delivering it.
But he who, having shown a faultless [article], delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double its price and an equal amount as a fine.
Likewise, he who, having sold an item into the hand of one person, delivers it to another,
shall be made to pay double that amount and shall be punished to the same extent.
If a buyer does not accept a commodity being offered for sale,
or if a seller sells it elsewhere after having already sold it, neither of them shall be held at fault.
This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
if it is not delivered, except by mutual agreement, there is no transgression on the part of the seller.
N8.11 For merchants, buying and selling all kinds of merchandise is for the sake of profit;
and that profit, having depended upon the price, may either become great or not.
Therefore, at the proper place and time, a merchant should strive to determine the market price;
he should not proceed by dishonest means, for such is the superior path of trade.
9. Non-delivery after sale (vikrīyāsaṃpradāna).
When a buyer, having purchased a commodity for its price, does not regard it as satisfactory, this legal subject is called "repentance after purchase" (krītvānuśaya).
If, after having purchased a commodity for a price, the buyer considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is still unspoiled.
If the buyer delivers [the property] on the second day, he shall pay a thirtieth part of the price as a fine;
on the third day, that fine shall be double; after that, it belongs to the buyer alone.
The purchaser should personally examine the merchandise beforehand for its merits and defects;
once it has been examined, approved, and purchased, it shall not be returned to the seller.
One should examine a milch cow for three days, but a draft animal for five days;
however, the examination of pearls, diamonds, and corals should last for seven days.
For bipeds, the impurity shall last half a month for males and twice that for females;
for all seeds, it lasts ten days; for metals and clothes, one day.
Furthermore, a garment that has been worn, which is soiled, stained,
and even defective, once sold, shall not belong to the seller again.
For a garment that has been washed once, one-eighth of its value is lost;
for a second time, one-half; for a third time, one-third; and for a fourth time, indeed one-half [of the remaining value].

But beyond the point where half has been exhausted, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter at each stage, until it reaches the state of being worn out with its ten parts diminished; for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding further decay.
N9.10a: For all metals as well, the cause [of their transformation] is the application of fire in the process of working;
N9.10c: it is observed that when they are being refined, their impurities are destroyed through contact with fire.
There is no loss in the case of gold; for silver, there is a loss of two palas per hundred;
it should be known that for tin and lead, the loss shall be eight palas per hundred.
One should know that five palas [of impurity] are found in copper, as well as in whatever products are made from it;
because there are many varieties of that metal, there is no fixed rule regarding the loss of iron.
In the processing of woven cloth, the loss and gain have been declared;
for threads made of cotton or wool, the increase is ten palas per hundred.
For those [threads] of medium thickness, like thick yarns, the internal loss is declared to be one hundred and five;
however, for very fine threads, it is declared to be three palas.
The loss for a debt incurred by labor on woolen cloth (*romaviddha*) is one-thirtieth;
however, for silk (*kauṣeya*) and bark garments (*valkala*), there is neither increase nor loss.
A merchant who is skilled in commodities should not harbor regret after having purchased;
rather, he should understand the increase and decrease of goods as well as their market availability.
The established practice of heretics, guilds, and other such groups is called a *samaya* (convention). The non-fulfillment of such a convention is recorded as a ground for legal dispute.
The king should likewise protect the established conventions among heretics, guilds, corporations, associations, bands, and assemblies, both within the fort and in the countryside.
Whatever their duty, whatever their action, whatever the rule for their attendance,
and whatever their means of livelihood— let him approve of all that accordingly.
Whatever is contrary to the king's will, whatever is inherently contemptible, and whatever is detrimental to his interests— he should turn that away from them.
The king shall not tolerate their mutual forming of confederacies, the carrying of weapons for harmful purposes, or their mutual injury.
Those who would divide the separate groups must be especially disciplined;
for if they are neglected, they will bring about terrible danger, like a disease.
Whatever ritual act should be defective because it is not prescribed by the sacred tradition,
even if it has already been commenced, a king who desires his own welfare must cause it to be stopped.
Where there are determinations regarding embankments, field boundaries, limits, cultivated land, and uncultivated land— such matters pertaining to fields constitute a dispute arising from fields.
In disputes concerning the boundaries of fields, the decision shall be based on the testimony of the neighbors,
as well as those who are the heads of cities, villages, or guilds, and those men who are the most venerable.
And those who live by agriculture outside the boundaries of the village,
as well as cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and others who dwell in the forest.
They should mark out the boundary, characterized by signs such as husks,
charcoal, potsherds, jars, sanctuaries, and trees.
And by means of well-known anthills, level and uneven ground, and the like;
as well as by ancient fields, gardens, paths, and embankments.
In the case of lands whose boundaries have been carried away by rivers, abandoned, or lost,
[the boundary] shall be determined by inferring those locations through measurements and by observing long-standing possession.
If, however, the neighbors should speak falsely in determining that matter,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
But others, such as the heads of guilds and the like, should be made to pay fines individually;
if they persist in falsehood, they should be punished with the first amercement.
A single man, even if he is highly trustworthy, shall not determine a boundary;
because of the gravity of this legal matter, this procedure is established upon many witnesses.
If there is only one person to mark the boundary, he should do so while fasting and composed in mind,
wearing red garlands and garments, and placing the earth upon his head.
But when there are no knowers of the boundary and no boundary markers,
then the king himself shall determine the boundary between the two parties as he deems fit.
By this very same rule, the procedure for legal disputes concerning houses, gardens, water reservoirs, dwellings, and so forth, as well as those between different villages, has been declared.
One should not obstruct crossroads, temples, carriage-roads, or paths with refuse-heaps, ground-level pits, chasms, drains, and the like.
A watercourse built across another's field is not prohibited, provided it brings great benefit and causes little harm; for when there is a loss [to one], an increase [in yield] is desired.

A dam, moreover, should be known to be of two kinds: one to be dug out (kheya) and likewise one to be built (bandhya). That which is to be dug out is for the purpose of directing the flow of water, while that which is to be built is for the purpose of stopping it.
Without water, the crop would perish; yet by excessive water it likewise perishes. That very same fault which exists in the absence of water is recorded as existing in the case of excessive water.
But whoever should construct a new embankment over one that was previously established and has fallen into ruin, without having first consulted the owner, shall not partake in its fruit.
But when the owner has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is a human being,
one should then undertake that work of constructing a bridge after having petitioned the king.
Otherwise, one would incur affliction by observing the deer-hunter;
for the arrows of him who pierces again what has already been pierced are lost.
If the owner of the field is unable, deceased, or lost, and no one prevents it,
if someone should cultivate the field, he shall enjoy its fruit.
If the owner of a field returns while it is being ploughed,
he shall recover his own field by paying for all the cultivation of the fallow land.
Then, by a reduction of one-eighth each year until seven years have passed,
when the eighth year is reached, he shall recover possession of the cultivated field.
After one year, it becomes half-waste; after three years, it becomes waste;
but a field neglected for five years shall be equal to a wilderness.
A field that has been held by three generations, or a house that has come down by succession—
with the exception of what is granted by royal favor— one should not allow another to take away the enjoyment of such property.
But where cattle or other animals cause damage to crops by crossing over a fence,
the keeper shall be punished there, provided he did not prevent it to the best of his ability.
But in the case of the destruction of standing crops along with their roots, the owner of the field shall receive an equivalent amount;
the herdsman shall be released from liability by the killing [of the offending animal], and he shall inflict the fine upon the owner.
A cow that has recently calved, as well as bulls, goats, sheep, and elephants, must be kept away [from the field] with great effort for ten days; their owner shall not be subject to punishment.
He should cause a cow to pay a fine of one māṣa, and likewise a buffalo two māṣas;
for a goat or a sheep that has a young with it, the fine shall be half a māṣa.
Elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are considered the protectors of the subjects;
likewise, a cow that is pregnant, one that has recently calved, and one that is in heat are exempt from punishment.
But for those who sit down twice [to eat], it is declared to be double; however, if she remains [there], it is fourfold.
For those who act as direct supervisors, the punishment for theft is likewise ordained by tradition.
If cows that have strayed due to the fault of the herdsman take refuge in a field, there is no punishment for the owner of the cattle; the herdsman deserves that punishment.
Or seized by a king’s grasping, or even struck by a thunderbolt;
or bitten by a serpent, or even fallen from the summit of a mountain.
If [the animal] is killed by a lion or a tiger, or struck down by diseases,
there is no fault on the part of the keeper, nor is there any fault on the part of the owners.
If a man seeks to recover grain that has been eaten by cows,
the neighbor must pay the value of the crop that was sown there;
however, fodder for the cows must be given to the owner of the cattle, while the grain itself belongs to the cultivator.
If a field located at the edge of a village, at the boundary of a pasture, or on a high road is uncovered,
there is no fault on the part of the guardian if it is destroyed.
On the roadside, a fence should be constructed such that a camel cannot look over it,
nor can an animal, a horse, or a boar jump over or break through it.
A house and a field should be understood as the basis for the residence of householders;
therefore, the king should not confiscate them, for they are the very root of householders.
When the realm prospers, the king’s righteousness and treasury increase;
when it declines, they too diminish. Therefore, he should rely upon the causes of prosperity.
That section of legal dispute where the rules for the marriage and other rites of women and men are proclaimed is called the title of law known as "The Union of Man and Woman."
But for a man and a woman, the formal choosing (varaṇa) is prescribed first;
after the choosing comes the grasping of the hand, and then the sacramental rite (saṃskāra) which possesses two characteristics.
N12.3a: For those two, the status of being a wife is said to be indefinite because of the perception of defects;
N12.3c: it becomes definite through the taking of the hand and the recitation of the mantras, which constitute the defining characteristic of a wife.
In the case of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, a wife of their own caste is superior;
and for a woman, a husband of her own caste is likewise superior.
A Brāhmaṇa may have three other wives in the direct order [of castes],
while a Śūdra woman may likewise have three other husbands in the inverse order.
Two wives for a Kṣatriya and one for a Vaiśya are proclaimed;
two husbands are to be known for a Vaiśya woman, and one other for a Kṣatriya woman.
Up to the seventh or the fifth degree from the paternal and maternal relatives,
those who share the same *gotra* as well as those who have the same *pravara* are ineligible for marriage.
A man must be examined regarding his virility by the very characteristics of his own limbs;
if he is proven to be a man without exception, he is fit to receive a maiden.
His collarbones, knees, and bones are well-knit; his shoulders and neck are firmly set; his temples are broad, his thighs are slender, his skin is thin, and his gait and voice are unhindered.
If his feces float in water and his urine is pleasant-smelling and frothy, he shall be a male by these characteristics; however, if they are the opposite, he is a eunuch (paṇḍaka).
In the treatise, that [doubt] is seen by the wise to be of fourteen kinds;
the method for treating those that are curable and those that are incurable has been stated in due order.
One born impotent, one who becomes so through castration, and likewise one who is impotent for a period of time;
as well as those rendered so by the curse of a guru, by disease, or by the wrath of the gods.
The jealous man (īrṣyāpaṇḍa), the one who must be served (sevya), the one with wind-semen (vātaretas), the one whose vulva is in the mouth (mukhebhaga), the one who is rejected (ākṣipta),
the one with futile seed (moghabīja), the modest man (śālīna), and likewise the one whose master is another (anyapati).
Among these, the first two are incurable; the one called *pakṣaka* should be treated for a month.
For this triad, the duration is traditionally recorded as one year in successive order.
The other four [defects] that have been mentioned— jealousy, impotence, and so forth—
must be abandoned by a woman whose womb has been damaged, just as they are by one who has fallen from her caste.
If her husband has been incapacitated by a curse or is impotent, and he makes no effort to remedy the situation,
another man is permitted for the woman after she has waited for one year.
Even for a man of refined character (*śālīna*), the banner (*dhvaja*) is brought low by union with a bold woman;
therefore, one should employ other women, young girls, and the like to diminish his passion.
If a man who is devoted to another woman becomes unfaithful toward his own wife, she may take another husband; this is the ordinance of Prajāpati.
Women were created for the sake of offspring; a woman is the field, and progeny belongs to the owner of the seed.
The field should be given to one who possesses seed; one without seed does not deserve the field.
The father himself, or the brother with the father’s consent, the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, as well as kinsmen and relatives, may give away the maiden.
But in the absence of a mother, if she [the father] remains in his natural state toward all [sons],
they shall give the girl in marriage from their own caste when she is no longer in her natural state [i.e., has reached puberty].
But when there is no one at all [suitable], the maiden should approach the king;
with his permission, having obtained a suitor, she may choose him herself.
He should practice dharma together with one who is of the same caste and similar in family, appearance, age, and learning; and from her, he should procreate sons.
If a man, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country,
the maiden may choose another groom after three menstrual seasons have passed.
If a maiden should neglect her dancing, she must inform her relatives;
if they do not give her to a husband, they shall be equal to killers of embryos (bhrūṇahan).
As many seasons as have passed for her while she is without a husband,
so many instances of foeticide shall belong to him who does not give her back.
Therefore, before the menses have begun, the father should give away his daughter once;
otherwise, a great sin would touch him, for this is the rule of the virtuous.
A share of inheritance falls [to one] but once; a daughter is given in marriage but once; "I give"—this is said but once. These three things happen only once each.
The rule for these five marriages, beginning with the Brāhma, is recorded in the tradition;
however, in the three beginning with the Āsura, the giving [of the bride] depends upon [the groom's] qualities.
If a bridegroom who has received the bride-price should arrive when the girl is already of marriageable age,
a statement made there that is consistent with dharma, artha, and kāma would not be considered false.
One should not defile an unblemished maiden, nor should one defile an unblemished bridegroom;
however, if a defect exists, there shall be no offense for the two of them if they mutually abandon one another.
If a man, having given a maiden to a suitor in accordance with the law,
does not hand her over to him while the suitor remains blameless, he shall be punished by the king like a thief.
But for him who gives away a girl in marriage without disclosing her defects,
the king shall inflict the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence.
But if a man, out of malice, declares a girl to be "not a virgin" without demonstrating any fault in her, he shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
But if a groom, having accepted an unblemished maiden, should abandon her—
even against his will— he must be punished and compelled to marry that very same girl.

Being tall, being afflicted by loathsome diseases, being deformed, having had sexual intercourse, and being impudent or having her affections fixed on another— these are proclaimed as the defects of a maiden.

One who is insane, one who has fallen from his caste, a eunuch, one who is unfortunate, one who has abandoned his kin, and the two defects previously mentioned regarding a maiden— this collection of defects applies to the groom.
Eight forms of marriage have been proclaimed for the sacramental refinement of the social classes;
among them, the Brāhma and likewise the Prājāpatya are the first.
The Ārṣa, the Daiva, the Gāndharva, and likewise the Āsura;
the Rākṣasa follows immediately after that, while the Paiśāca is recorded as the eighth.
Having honored the bride and invited her, one should give her away adorned in the Brāhma form;
the Prājāpatya rite is prescribed as that in which one says, "May you both perform your duty together."
Having given a pair of a cow and a bull, the marriage is called Ārṣa;
but that which takes place within the sacrificial enclosure for the officiating priest performing the ritual is Daiva.
When he desires a woman who desires him, they call that the fifth [form of marriage], named Gāndharva;
whereas the Āsura form of marriage is to be known by the practice of giving a bride-price (śulka).
The Rākṣasa form of marriage is said to result from abduction by force;
the eighth and lowest is the Paiśāca, resulting from approaching a woman while she is asleep or intoxicated.
Of these, the four beginning with the Brāhma [marriage] are declared to be lawful;
the Gāndharva is common to all, while the three following it are unlawful.
But other women who have had previous husbands are said to be of seven kinds in their proper order:
among them, the *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) is of three types, while the *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman) is of four types.

A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the grasping of the hand [in marriage], is called the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman); she is eligible for the sacramental rite once again.
She who, having abandoned her husband from her youth, resorts to another man and then returns to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second [type].
When there are no brothers-in-law, a woman who is given by her kinsmen to a man of the same caste who is not a sapinda is proclaimed as the third [form of marriage].
A woman, whether she has borne children or not,
who out of desire resorts to another man while her husband is still alive, is the first type of unchaste woman (svairiṇī).
When her husband has died, she who rejects even the brothers-in-law who have approached her and,
out of desire, goes to another man is proclaimed as the second [type of remarried woman].
She who has come from another country, who has been purchased with wealth, and who is afflicted by hunger and thirst,
having approached saying "I am yours"— she is proclaimed as the third [type of wife].
A woman who, having been given by her elders in accordance with local customs,
subsequently commits an act of violence against another man, is indeed declared to be a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman).
This rule has been proclaimed for women who have remarried and for wanton women;
among these, each preceding one is inferior, while each succeeding one is superior.
The offspring of one who has been acquired for a price belongs to the progenitor;
however, in the case of one who has come to him without a price, that fruit belongs solely to the owner of the field.
If seed is sown in a field without the knowledge of the owner of the field, there is no share for the owner of the seed; that [crop] belongs to the owner of the field alone.
If seed carried by a flood or the wind sprouts in someone’s field, that field-owner shall enjoy the fruit;
the owner of the seed shall not share in the fruit.
If a great bull, while roaming among the cows in another's pen, should father calves, those calves belong to him whose cows they are; the bull's seed has been spent in vain.
If seed sown with the owner of the field’s consent is produced in that field,
that offspring is considered to belong to both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field.
There can be no crop without a field, nor does it exist without a seed;
therefore, according to the law, offspring is held to belong to both the father and the mother.

When a woman who has a protector is seen by experts in the law engaged with a man in another's house, that is considered adultery; however, it is not so if she has come to his own house of her own accord.
There is no offense of violence against one who approaches the wife of a man who is corrupt, has abandoned his wife, is impotent, or is submissive, provided he does so of his own will.

Standing together with another man’s wife at an improper time or in an improper place, or conversing with her, or engaging in dalliance— these three are the stages of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
At the confluence of rivers, at sacred fords, in groves, and in forests— if a woman and a man meet there, it shall be considered adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*) and they should be apprehended.
By sending female messengers, by dispatching letters,
and by other such transgressions, all such acts are recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or likewise, if he is touched by her and consents to it, that shall constitute *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) with mutual consent.
Whether by means of edibles, or foods, or likewise by garments, garlands,
and perfumes sent as gifts— all this is recorded in tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (seduction).
Whether out of pride, delusion, or self-praise, if he should say of his own accord,
"This woman was previously enjoyed by me," all such cases are recorded in the law as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
He who seizes her by the hand, or by the braid of hair, or even by the edge of her garment;
or he who says, "Stay! Stay!", all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual assault).
When men violate their own caste, the highest amercement has been prescribed;
in the reverse case, however, it is the middle amercement, but in the case of inverse order (prātiloma), it is death.
If the maiden is unwilling, there shall be the amputation of two fingers;
however, in the case of a woman of the highest caste, there shall indeed be execution as well as the confiscation of all her property.
But if the maiden is willing and he is of the same caste, there is no transgression; however, having adorned her and honored her, he alone shall marry her.
A mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife,
a paternal aunt, the wife of a paternal uncle, a friend’s wife, a female disciple, a sister, her female friend, and a daughter-in-law.
A daughter, the wife of a teacher, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
Having approached any one of these women, one is called a violator of the Guru’s bed;
the punishment therein is the excision of the penis, and no other is prescribed.
One who violates a female animal should be punished with a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
for cows, the middle amercement is prescribed, and the same applies to women of the lowest castes.
The punishment urged by the king instructs him who approaches a woman who should not be approached;
in this matter, however, purification through the prescribed rite of atonement is the means of cleansing.

A woman who is self-willed, a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, a courtesan, a female slave, and one who has left her husband— all these women may be approached in the direct order of the castes, but never in the inverse order.
But with these very same female slaves, there would be a fault as great as with the wives of others;
for even if they are approachable, one should not have intercourse with them if they belong to another.
If the husband of a woman who has not yet borne children should die, she,
being authorized by her elders, may approach her brother-in-law out of a desire for offspring.
And he should undertake that [rite] in the same manner from the birth of a son;
when a son is born, it should cease, for otherwise there would be a transgression.
Having anointed his limbs with clarified butter or unrefined oil,
avoiding the contact of mouth with mouth and the touching of limb with limb;

He should not approach a woman who already has a son, one who is barren, one who has ceased to menstruate, one who is unwilling, one who is pregnant, one who is censurable, or one who has not been authorized by her kinsmen.
But if a woman not authorized by her husband should bear a son through her brother-in-law,
those who speak according to the Dharma say that he is born of an adulterer and is not entitled to the inheritance.
Likewise, if a younger brother approaches the wife of his elder brother without authorization,
or if an elder brother approaches the wife of his younger brother, both of them are guilty of violating the Guru’s bed.

But when the family line has been reduced to a single survivor, one who is appointed by his elders may approach the wife of his younger brother for the sake of continuing the lineage, and not out of lust.
But when the teacher is not present, the king should be informed of the destruction of the family;
then, having instructed her, he may depart with the woman at his word.
Having bathed according to the very procedure previously described during the *puṃsavana* rite, the pure husband [should approach her];
or rather, until the *garbhādhāna* is performed, she is like a daughter-in-law once conception has occurred.
Therefore, a man or even a woman who, out of desire, behaves otherwise than this, should be severely punished by the king; for by failing to restrain them, he would become a sinner.
But when a quarrel arises between a husband and wife due to jealousy, malice, or passion, they should dispute it among themselves, not before kinsmen nor before the king.

If a man and a woman who are mutually opposed abandon each other, there shall be no sin for the man; however, this is not the case for the woman, except when she has committed adultery while her husband was concealed from her.
In the event of infidelity, the woman shall undergo shaving of the head, sleeping on the ground, eating wretched food, wearing poor clothing, and performing the labor of clearing away refuse.
A woman who has squandered her husband's wealth, one who has lost all her property, one who causes a miscarriage,
or one who desires the death of her husband, he shall banish from the home.
A wise man should expel from the home that wife who is constantly inclined toward what is harmful, who speaks unpleasantly, and who eats before her husband.
One should not, out of desire, take pleasure in a barren woman, one who gives birth only to daughters, one who is censurable, or one who is always hostile; by acting in this way, he incurs guilt.
If a man abandons a wife who is compliant, not foul-mouthed, capable, virtuous, and has borne children, he shall be punished by the king with a heavy fine.

If a woman has been carried off by one who was unaware of her fault, and she has not taken refuge with another, she must be restored by her kinsmen; if she has no kinsmen, she herself should seek refuge.
When the husband has disappeared, died, renounced the world, become impotent, or fallen from his caste—
under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women.

A Brāhmaṇa woman whose husband has gone abroad should wait for eight years if she has not borne a child; but if she has borne a child, she should wait for four years, after which she may resort to another man.

A Kṣatriya woman who has not borne children may remain for six years; one who has borne children may remain for three years. A Vaiśya woman who has borne children may remain for four years, while another [a Śūdra woman] should live for two years.
No specific time limit is prescribed for a Śūdra woman, nor is there a transgression of dharma [if she remains longer];
however, for one who has not borne a child, her stay [in the house of her husband] is limited to one year.
This rule regarding women whose husbands have gone abroad is prescribed for cases where there has been no contact;
however, if he is heard to be alive, this procedure shall be doubled.
In the production of offspring, this is the creation of beings by Prajāpati;
therefore, when women go to another [man] for this purpose, no such fault exists.
The birth of the social orders (varṇas) in the natural order is known as the established rule;
that which occurs in the reverse order is to be understood as a mixture of castes (varṇasaṃkara).

The son born of a woman one degree lower is declared to be *anantara*; likewise, the son born of a woman two degrees lower is *ekāntara*, and the son born of a woman three degrees lower is *dvyantara*—this being according to the natural order (*anuloma*), and the same applies to the inverse order (*pratiloma*).
The Ugra, the Pāraśava, and the Niṣāda are proclaimed as the three sons of Śūdra women born from the three highest castes in the direct order of succession.
From a Brāhmaṇa woman, moreover, there are the Caṇḍāla, the Sūta, and the Vaidehaka;
these three others are to be known as born from the three [lower castes] in the inverse order.
The Ambaṣṭha, the Māgadha, and the Kṣattṛ are the sons of a Kṣatriya woman;
among these, one is born in the natural order (ānulomya) and two are to be known as born in the inverse order (pratiloma).
The sons of a Vaiśya woman, however, are the Dauṣṣanta, Yavana, and Āyogava;
among these, one is born from the reverse order (prātilomya) and two are to be known as born from the natural order (anuloma).

Those born in the reverse order of castes, such as the Sūta and others, who are produced through the inverse sequence of birth, are known as *saṃkara*s; beginning with the Śvapāka, their group consists of twenty-one members.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a wife of equal caste is a Savarṇa; from a Kṣatriya wife, he is an Anantara.
Likewise, the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are the two sons of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya respectively.
But the son of a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman is the Dauṣṣanta, separated by one interval;
likewise, from a Kṣatriya with a Śūdra woman, there is born the one named Niṣāda.
A Śūdra woman bears to a Brāhmaṇa a Pāraśava son, who is superior [to her father]; for these are proclaimed to be the sons born according to the natural order (ānulomya) of the castes.
The Sūta, the Māgadha, and likewise the Āyogava— these sons born from the castes in the reverse order are similarly immediate [in their descent].
The Sūta is declared to be the son born immediately after [the Kṣatriya] from a Brāhmaṇa woman;
likewise, the Māgadha and the Āyogava are the two sons of the Vaiśya and the Śūdra respectively.
A Brāhmaṇa woman bears to a Vaiśya a son called a Vaidehaka, who is one degree lower;
likewise, a Kṣatriya woman bears to a Śūdra a son called a Kṣattṛ, who is also one degree lower.

A son born from a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother through such a transgression of the natural order is a Cāṇḍāla, the most wicked among those born of mixed castes (saṃkara), provided that the Brāhmaṇī has been deluded.
The king must investigate so that no intermixture of castes occurs;
therefore, the king must especially protect the three [Vedas] from such confusion.
Where the partition of paternal property is carried out by sons,
that is declared by the wise to be the legal subject matter known as *dāyabhāga* (partition of inheritance).
N13.2 When the father has died, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth;
in the absence of daughters, the daughters [inherit], and in their absence, the offspring of those daughters.

Or rather, the father himself, having reached old age, should divide his sons,
giving the eldest a superior share, or according to whatever his own inclination may be.
The eldest brother should support all [the others] who desire it, just as a father does;
or a capable younger brother may do so, for in a family, religious rites depend upon one's ability.

Excluding the property acquired through valor, the wife, and inherited wealth, as well as whatever may be the wealth acquired through learning— these three are indivisible, as is any gift from a paternal ancestor.
And for one to whom his mother has given her own property out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply; the mother is as beloved as the father.

That which is received in the presence of the sacred fire, that which is received at the wedding, as well as the gift from the husband, and [that received] from brothers, mother, and father— this sixfold property is declared to be the woman's separate wealth (strīdhana).

The woman’s property goes to her offspring, and if she has no offspring, it goes to the husband; however, in the case of the four [forms of marriage] beginning with the Brāhma, they say it goes to the father, while in the others, it goes to the husband.
He who maintains the family of a brother who is acquiring learning shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself is unlearned.
A learned man shall not, against his will, give a share from his own wealth to one who is unlearned,
unless that wealth was acquired by him while relying upon the paternal estate.
When dividing his own property, a father may take two shares for himself;
the mother shall be entitled to an equal share with the sons once her husband has died.
A larger share than the standard portion should be given to the eldest, for it is traditionally taught that a special boon belongs to the eldest;
the remaining brothers shall share the estate equally, as shall an unmarried sister.
Likewise, among sons born according to the law from women of lower castes,
there is a gradual reduction of the share for those born of wives who were duly married.
But for those who have been divided by the father himself with unequal shares of wealth—whether less, more, or equal—the same rule shall apply to them; for the father is the master of all.
The son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), and he who is born of a woman concealed [in secret]— of these,
the man who marries them is to be known as the father, and they are declared to be entitled to a share of the inheritance.
He who has an unknown father and is born of an unmarried woman (kānīna) shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his property.
Those who are born of a woman not authorized [to bear children], whether by one man or by many, are all non-inheritors;
they are the sons of the biological fathers alone.
They shall give the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the biological father if the mother was obtained through a marriage fee (śulka);
but if she was approached without a fee, those cakes belong to the husband alone.
One who hates his father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who is born of adultery—even these sons of the body (aurasa) shall not receive a share; how much less so those born of the wife (kṣetraja)?

Those afflicted by long-lasting or severe illness, as well as the mentally dull, the insane, the blind, and the lame, should be maintained within the family; however, their sons shall be entitled to a share of the inheritance.
N13.22 Those who are *dvairāmuṣyāyaṇas* (belonging to two lineages) should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and water separately to both [fathers].
Likewise, they should take half a share from the inheritance for the benefit of both the biological father (*bījika*) and the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*).
But the share belonging to those who are reunited (saṃsṛṣṭin) is prescribed for them alone;
otherwise, among those without offspring, the heirs shall go to the others as sharers of the portion.
If among brothers one should die without offspring, or if he should enter the religious life,
the remaining brothers shall divide his property, excluding the woman’s separate property.
They shall provide for his maintenance and for that of the women until the end of their lives;
however, if they preserve the bed of their husband, they shall receive it, but in other cases, they shall forfeit it.
N13.26a. Whosoever has a daughter, the paternal share is considered her portion for maintenance. N13.26c. Until her marriage, he should support her; thereafter, the husband shall maintain her.
When her husband has died, the husband's kin are the masters of a woman who has no son;
they are the authority over her employment and protection, and they are the ones responsible for her maintenance.
When the husband’s family is completely exhausted, devoid of men, and without support, and when his *sapiṇḍas* no longer exist, the father’s side is the authority over the woman.
But at the conclusion of both [the husband's] life and his failure in duty, the king is declared to be the woman's protector;
he shall provide for her maintenance and restrain her if she deviates from the path.
N13.30 Even women born into noble families perish through independence;
therefore, Prajāpati ordained that they lack independence.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in widowhood; a woman does not deserve independence.
Whatever remains after the father’s debts have been paid from the paternal inheritance must be divided by the brothers, so that the father would not remain a debtor.
And for those whose purificatory rites were not performed in due order by their father,
those rites must be performed by their brothers from the paternal wealth itself.
If paternal wealth is not available,

the consecratory rites that must necessarily be performed for brothers who have not yet been consecrated should be carried out by those who have already been consecrated, using funds drawn from their own shares.
He who is engaged in the affairs of the family and performs those duties should be supported by his brothers with food, clothing, and transport.

When there is doubt regarding the law of partition among heirs, the decision is reached through kinsmen and written records of the shares, as well as by the separate performance of their respective affairs.
Among brothers who have not divided their inheritance, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has taken place, their religious duties shall also become distinct for each.

The giving and receiving [of property], the possession of livestock, food, houses, and fields, as well as the cooking, religious duties, income, and expenditures of those who have been partitioned, should be understood as distinct for each.
Witnessing, acting as a guarantor, giving, and receiving—
these brothers who have divided their inheritance may perform among themselves, but not those who have not divided.
Those among whose own heirs these transactions proceed in the world—
one should recognize them as divided, even in the absence of a written document.
If many sons born of one [father] have separate religious duties, separate activities,
and are endowed with separate qualities of action, they are not considered eligible for joint undertakings.
If they should give their own shares, or even sell them, they may do all that as they wish; for they are masters of their own property.

The legitimate son (aurasa), the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra), as well as the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with the bride (sahoḍha), and likewise the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna).

The son of a remarried woman, the abandoned son, the received son, the purchased son, the made son, and likewise the son who has come of his own accord— these are declared to be the twelve kinds of sons.
Among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs;
each preceding one is declared superior, and each succeeding one inferior.
For these would inherit that wealth after the father has died in due order;
in the absence of each elder brother, the younger one shall obtain it.
In the absence of a son, however, the daughter [inherits] because she is seen to provide an equal continuation of the lineage;
for both the son and the daughter are declared to be the continuators of the father's line.

But in the absence of daughters, the kinsmen (sakulyas) shall take it, and after them the relatives (bāndhavas); then those of the same caste (sajātyas). In the absence of all these, it goes to the king.
Except for a Brāhmaṇa, however, the king devoted to righteousness shall provide maintenance for women; this is recorded as the rule for inheritance.
Whatever act is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength is called *sāhasa* (violence); here, *saha* is said to mean strength.
Furthermore, that [discipline] is to be known as threefold—namely, the first, the middle, and likewise the highest; its specific characteristics have been stated separately in the treatises.
The destruction, seizure, or crushing of fruits, roots, water, and other such things, as well as the implements of cultivation, is declared to be the first degree of *sāhasa* (violence).
Regarding clothing, livestock, food, drink, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle-level fine (madhyama-sāhasa) is prescribed.
Malice, the use of poison or weapons, the violation of another's wife, and whatever else is said to be life-threatening constitute the highest amercement (uttama-sāhasa).
The punishment for the first [offense] depends on the nature of the act and shall not be less than one hundred;
however, according to those learned in the treatises, the punishment for the middle [offense] should be known as not less than five hundred.

Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding, and the amputation of that specific limb— these are declared to be the punishments for the highest degree of violence (uttama-sāhasa).
This rule of punishment is ordained for all without distinction; however, except for death, a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve execution. A Brāhmaṇa is not worthy of being put to death.
The punishment for him shall be the shaving of the head, banishment from the city,
the branding of the mark of his crime upon the forehead, and being led away on a donkey.
Those two may be considered fit for social intercourse if they have been punished for the first two [offenses];
however, even one who has been punished for the highest violence (uttamasāhasa) should be known as one with whom no social communion (asaṃbhojya) is permitted.

Theft shall be considered a specific variety of that very [crime]; its distinction is stated therein: they call it *atisāhasa* (excessive violence) when committed by force, but theft (*steya*) when committed by fraud.
That [punishment] is also declared by the wise to be threefold, depending on the nature of the object:
namely, from the seizure of objects that are low, middling, or superior.
Earthenware vessels, seats, beds, bones, wood, leather, grass, and the like,
as well as small grains such as *śamī* and *mudga*, are declared to be minor property (*kṣudradravya*).
Clothing, except for silk; likewise cattle, except for cows;
iron, except for gold; and also rice and barley—these constitute the middle class [of property].
Gold, gems, silk, women, bulls, elephants, and horses,
as well as the property of gods, Brahmins, and kings, should be known as the highest category of goods.
The wise declare that theft consists of the removal of these [goods] by deceiving them through various means, or from those who are asleep, careless, or intoxicated.
Theft is established by the seizure of stolen goods; even in the absence of such goods, it is proven through the act of consumption.
Suspicion arises from association with wicked persons, as well as from irregularities in income and expenditure.
Those who provide food and shelter to thieves as they move about, and those who,
though capable, look on with indifference, are also partakers in that guilt.
Moreover, when property is being carried off while people are crying out,
those who hear it and do not run to the rescue are also partakers in that offense.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed by the wise for the three types of violent crimes (sāhasa),
that same punishment applies also to theft (steya) of the three types of property, in their respective order.
When cattle or other such property have been lost or stolen,
people who are experts in the matter shall trace them by their tracks until the source is reached.
In a village, a cattle-pen, or a pasture, wherever the footprint may be found, it shall be carried by that person; unless he carries it elsewhere.
If the place is confused or ruined due to its unevenness,
or if it is near a village or a cattle-pen, one should discharge [the arrow] toward that which is closer.
When two people are on the same path, a person is generally considered impure by that [fact] if he has been seen previously in misdeeds, or if he has associated with evil-minded men.
In the villages, the Caṇḍālas, executioners, and others should conduct the search; likewise, those who roam outside at night should carry out the search outside.
If thieves cannot be apprehended, the king shall provide restitution from his own treasury; for by neglecting this, he becomes a sinner and falls away from both merit and wealth.

Speech that is contrary in meaning and joined with insults regarding one's country, caste, family, and so forth, as well as [insults concerning] bodily defects— that is called verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*).
N15-16.2a. Because of being harsh, vulgar, or excessive, that [abuse] is also recorded as being of three kinds.
N15-16.2c. According to the sequence of their gravity, the punishment here also increases accordingly.

That which is accompanied by an insult is to be known as "harsh" (niṣṭhura); that which is joined with a physical deformity is "indecent" (aślīla). The wise say that [abuse] involving censure with grounds for expulsion is "severe" (tīvra).
N15-16.4a-c. Assaulting the limbs of another with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth, or injuring them with ashes and the like, is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (physical assault).
N15-16.5a. For that [offense] as well, three degrees are observed, namely mild, middling, and superior, respectively; N15-16.5c.
by means of threatening, striking without hesitation, and the appearance of wounds.

N15-16.6: For the transgression involving inferior, middling, and superior goods, they say there are exactly three types of *sāhasa* (violent crimes); therein lies the purification of the thorns [of the state].
The fivefold procedure has been declared for both of these [cases];
therein, purification and the liability to punishment are connected according to the circumstances.
When harshness arises from a fit of passion between two agitated parties,
he who shows forbearance is considered the one who bears the penalty, while he who oversteps is the offender.
When two [persons], both obscured by the fault of harshness, engage [in a dispute] simultaneously,
if no distinction can be perceived, the punishment for both shall be equal.
He who first insults another shall certainly bear the guilt;
he who does so afterwards is also a wrongdoer, but the punishment for the former is more severe.

If one person subsequently instigates two others who have already committed an offense against each other equally, he incurs the same punishment as either of those two, whether he was the first or the other.

N15-16.12. [One incurs the same sin] by having intercourse with a dog-cooker (śvapāka), a paṇḍaka, a caṇḍāla, or one who is deformed; with those who live by killing; with the wives of elephant-keepers, of outcasts (vrātya), or of a teacher (guru) and a preceptor (ācārya).
N15-16.13. When there is a transgression of established boundaries, immediate execution is the prescribed punishment;
and the wise say that this does not constitute the fault of physical assault.
For if these [officials] should transgress against a virtuous person among the subjects, that very person shall administer the punishment; the king does not incur the guilt for that punishment.
For these are indeed stains among men, and their wealth is of the nature of stain;
the king should have them executed, but he should not punish them with a fine.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya deserves one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brahmin should be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine should be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
For twice-born men of equal caste, the fine for transgression is twelve [paṇas] alone;
in the case of disputes that are not to be spoken of, that same amount shall be doubled.
If one speaks— even truthfully— of another as being one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly impaired, he shall be made to pay at least one *kārṣāpaṇa* by the king.

One should not, out of malice, disparage one who has performed purification according to the scriptures; nor should one disparage one punished by the king, for he would incur the penalty for such transgression.
In this world, two are proclaimed to be exempt from being spoken against and exempt from punishment:
the Brāhmaṇa and the king; for these two sustain this universe.
Having declared an outcast to be an outcast, or a thief to be a thief, one incurs an equal guilt by such speech; if the statement is false, one incurs double the guilt.
For a Śūdra who, out of malice, utters the name or caste of these [twice-born],
an iron spike eighteen finger-breadths long shall be driven into his body.
If he should out of pride give instruction in the Dharma to the twice-born,
the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
Whatever limb of a Brahmin by which a person of a lower caste may offend him, that very limb of his shall be cut off; in this way, he shall attain purification.

A man of lower birth who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of superior birth shall be banished after being branded on the hip with the mark of a dog's foot; or else, the king shall cause the region of his buttocks to be cut off.
If someone spits out of pride, the king shall cause both his lips to be cut off;
if he urinates upon him, his penis; and if he passes wind against him, his anus.
N15-16.28. If one seizes [the offender] by the hair, the king shall, without hesitation, have both his hands cut off;
likewise if he seizes him by the feet, the nose, the neck, or the testicles.
But having reviled a king who is established on his own path,
purification may be achieved either by the cutting off of the tongue or by the confiscation of all one's property.
But that evil-minded man who would strike the king, even though he has committed an offense,
shall be cooked on a spit in fire for longer than a hundred murders of Brahmins.
Neither a father for the offense of his son, nor a dog-owner for that of a dog,
nor a monkey-owner for that of a monkey shall be liable to punishment, provided they did not send them forth with those very [animals].
Gambling with dice, fists, stalks, and the like, played with deceit; betting games with birds, and other such contests—this is termed *dyūta* (gambling) and *samāhvaya* (betting).
The superintendent of the gambling house shall conduct the game and shall pay what is owed for it;
his fee for conducting the gambling shall be ten percent of the total.
When the dice fall twice in favor of the stake for a gambler,
they say that victory belongs to the other player and that the gambler has lost.
Gamblers should remain among gamblers when a dispute arises;
they alone shall be its observers, and they alone shall be the witnesses.
An impure gambler shall not resort to another gambling hall;
he shall not strike back at the master of the gaming house, nor shall he cause him to pay that [debt] according to his own will.
The king shall expel from the gambling hall those wicked men who play with fraudulent dice;
having placed a rosary of seeds around their necks, this is indeed declared to be their punishment.
Furthermore, in the miscellaneous section (prakīrṇaka), it should be known that legal proceedings (vyavahāra) concern those who rely upon the king:
namely, the defiance of the king's commands and likewise the failure to perform his duties.
The burning of cities, as well as the sowing of dissension among the subjects, and the subversion of the laws of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies; N18.2.
Disputes between father and son, transgression regarding penance,
the failure to accept gifts, and even anger on the part of those belonging to the stages of life (āśramas).
The defect of the intermixture of castes, as well as the restriction of their occupations,
and whatever was not seen in the previous [sections], all that shall be found in the *Prakīrṇaka*.
The king, however, being attentive, should protect all the stages of life (āśramas) by means of the four expedients prescribed in the treatises as well as those inherent [to his office].
Whichever caste should decline, or whichever should follow a state of excess—
seeing each of them deviated from their own path, he should establish them back upon the path.
And regarding other acts not prescribed by the scriptures that are joined with evil,
the king, having carefully considered them, shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
The king should not initiate that which is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti and detrimental to the people, nor should he allow it to continue once it has been initiated.
Whatever has been done by another king that is devoid of justice, and whatever has been done through ignorance—
that too, being established unjustly, he should bring back into accordance with justice.
Any man who does not observe the laws set forth by the king shall be punished as a sinner and,
for violating the royal decree, shall be subject to corporal punishment.
He shall take the weapons of those who live by arms, the draft animals and so forth of those who live by draft animals,
the ornaments of courtesans, and the musical instruments and their equipment from those skilled in them.
Whatever is the tool of anyone, by which artisans live their lives—
even when all their property is being confiscated— the king ought not to seize these.
He is without beginning and without end, the lord of the earth among bipeds;
for if he were not fallen from the path, he would be radiant and pure.
If the king did not administer punishment to all the social classes who have strayed from the path, these subjects would perish.
A Brahmin may abandon his status as a Brahmin, and a Kṣatriya may relinquish his Kṣatriya duties;
a Vaiśya may abandon his own specific occupation, but a Śūdra should distinguish himself from all others.
If there were no kings on earth to wield the rod of punishment,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
The constant favoring of the virtuous and likewise the restraint of the wicked—
this is recorded as the duty (*dharma*) of kings, as well as their purpose (*artha*), through the oppression of enemies.
Just as fire, though constantly burning these creatures,
is not defiled, so too the king, while inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it, is not defiled.
The authority of kings is their majesty, and that is established in their speech; whatever they may say, whether it be false or true, that is the law for those engaged in legal proceedings.
This one called the king moves upon the earth as the thousand-eyed Indra in person;
the subjects should never remain anywhere in defiance of his command.
Because he holds the office of protection, because of his sovereignty, and because he is seen to favor living beings, whatever the king ordains is authoritative; such is the established rule.
Just as a husband is always worthy of honor by women even if he is devoid of virtues,
so too is a lord of men worthy of honor by his subjects even if he is lacking in merit.
Subjects are purchased by the king through his asceticism; therefore, the monarch is their master.
Consequently, they must abide by his word, and their livelihood depends upon him.
Kings of immeasurable power possess five forms:
those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Dhanada.
When a protector of the earth, having fallen under the sway of anger, burns his subjects for some cause or even without cause, he is then said to be fire.
When a king, desiring victory, takes up arms and advances against his enemies by relying upon the element of fire (tejas), he is then described as being Indra.
When the king, free from the heat of anger and appearing joyful,
goes to see his subjects, he is then said to be Soma.
When the illustrious king, seated upon the throne of justice,
wields the rod of punishment with impartiality toward all beings, he is then Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
But when the lord of the earth favors suppliants, elders, the wise, servants, and others with gifts, then he is considered a giver of wealth (Dhanada).
Therefore, one should not despise him, nor revile him, nor treat him with contempt;
one should abide by his command, for death would result from its transgression.
His livelihood consists of protecting the subjects, serving the elderly and the wise, presiding over legal proceedings, and guarding himself.
A king, with a composed mind, should constantly attend upon Brahmins;
for the Kṣatriya power joined with Brahmins is the root of the protection of the world.
A Brahmin is exempt from the obligation of making way; a Kṣatriya may sit in front of him.
He is the first to be seen in the morning, and he receives salutations from all.

The first [portion] of the newly harvested grain belongs to him; likewise, he has the right of way when traveling. Furthermore, his entry into another's house for the purpose of begging alms is not forbidden.
N18.35ab/ Non-stealing consists in not taking fuel, flowers, or water that has been appropriated by another;
N18.35cd/ as well as not making demands on others and conversing with the wives of others.
On rivers, the crossing is free of tolls; likewise, one should cross first. On ferries, there is no payment of customs duty, provided that it is not his trade.
A Brāhmaṇa who is traveling on his journey, exhausted, and taking two stalks of sugarcane and five roots for himself while staying in no fixed abode, does not commit an offense.
One should not accept [gifts] from those who are accused, nor from outcasts, nor from enemies, nor from atheists;
nor from one who uses deception, nor for no reason, nor by causing distress to the donor.
Because of the great abundance of wealth and because they are worthy recipients,
accepting gifts from kings is superior [to receiving them] from others, with the exception of Brahmins.
Both the Brahmin and the king are observers of firm vows; there is no difference between these two, because both are devoted to the protection of the subjects and the dharma.
They say that the wealth of even a fierce king is pure, provided he knows the Dharma, is grateful, and rules for the sake of protecting those who are impure.
Just as the union of pure and impure waters attains equality in the ocean, so too does the influx of wealth for a king.
Just as gold placed in a blazing fire attains purity,
even so do all sacred traditions attain purification when they are among kings.
Whoever gives his own property to Brāhmaṇas, that must be permitted by the king as well; this is the eternal law.
From the land of a different kind than that which is customary, designated as the sixth part,
that tribute is ordained for him as the wages for protecting the subjects.
That which has been made over to one who is not a Brahmin can be taken back;
however, that which has been given to a Brahmin cannot be taken away again.
Giving, study, and sacrifice—these are his threefold duties; officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts constitute his means of livelihood, the third being the acceptance of gifts.
A twice-born man should remain established in his own duty and seek a livelihood that has been prepared;
he should not accept gifts from the unworthy among the social classes when they are lacking in self-restraint.
How is it that the king is not a deity— he by whose word an impure man becomes pure, and who instantly makes even a pure man impure?
Those twice-born ones who know the divinity of the king of immeasurable splendor are not defiled when they accept gifts from him.
In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, the sacrificial fire, gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise, a king as the eighth.
One should constantly behold these [images], pay homage to them, and worship them;
one should also circumambulate them, for in this way one's lifespan is not diminished.
The Supplement:
It should be known that there are two kinds of thieves who seize the property of others;
the self-possessed king should recognize them as both open and secret.
In that regard, those who deceive by means of light (i.e., open fraud),
those who rely on false weights and measures, those who take bribes, violent men, gamblers, and prostitutes [are all included].
Those who produce counterfeits and those who live by the pretext of auspicious rites—
such as these should be known as deceivers of the light of the world.
And those who dwell both outside and inside should be known as unmanifest;
they seize and plunder men while they are asleep or heedless.
Those who destroy districts, villages, or houses, those who waylay travelers on the road, and pickpockets— these and others like them should be known as secret thieves.
Having identified them through well-trained spies who perform those specific tasks,
they should be tracked down and apprehended by men stationed in secret.
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, taverns, and food-sellers; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles.
Empty houses, forests, and temples—
these must be scouted by spies who are intent on apprehending thieves.
In the same way, others who are well-disposed, trustworthy, and eloquent may act as spies;
for former thieves might incite those current thieves.
By means of providing food and drink, by attending social gatherings and festivals,
and likewise under the pretext of theft, they should bring about their meeting.
Those who do not approach there, even though they have been sent out and dispatched,
must be pursued and captured along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
Those thieves whom he may catch there, having beaten and humiliated them,
and having proclaimed their crime everywhere, they are to be executed by various modes of capital punishment.
But thieves who have not been caught red-handed and who do not reappear shall not be put to death by the king;
however, he should swiftly punish those caught in the act, along with their tools.
Those who strike at their own country, as well as those who obstruct the roads— having confiscated all their property, one should further inflict punishment upon them.
One should interrogate those caught as thieves on suspicion without violence;
through various forms of intimidation and stratagems, they shall speak of the matter exactly as it was done.
Regarding the place, time, direction, caste, name, or residence;
as well as the purpose and the laborers involved—these are the matters that must be questioned when determining the suppression of the offense.
Because of differences in color, voice, and appearance; because of reporting with uncertainty;
because of being seen at an improper place or time; and because of not clearing oneself even regarding one's clothing.
Because of the disappearance of what was not there before, because of prior theft, and because of association with those who do not exist [as honest people],
one should be understood even by slight signs, and not solely by the seizure of stolen goods (hoḍha).
If there should be suspicion against a man who follows the way of bandits, or even against a thief,
and if he should be touched by even a slight [taint], then an ordeal must be administered.
Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who supply fire and water,
those who give lodging, those who act as guides, and likewise those who provide assistance;
Purchasers of goods, as well as those who receive them, are declared by law to be subject to the same punishment,
as are those who conceal them.
In the provinces, those appointed as provincial governors and the neighboring chieftains who have been incited,
remaining neutral during times of attack— they are exactly like thieves.
If property is stolen within the jurisdiction of a person, that person must diligently search for the thieves;
otherwise, he shall be made to pay the value of the theft, unless the trail has disappeared.
But when that footprint has departed, vanished, or been cast elsewhere,
he should cause the neighbors, the road-keepers, and the guardians of the quarters to be made to pay.
If a house is indeed robbed, the king shall cause the village guards and the district officials to pay for it,
provided that the thief is not apprehended.
Or, if there is doubt regarding those being compelled to pay in respect to that theft,
the one who claims to have been robbed shall be made to swear an oath for the purpose of clearing himself of the charge of theft.
If a person who is not a thief is made to pay for a theft on the grounds of clearing himself of the charge of theft,
they shall, upon the actual thief being apprehended, be made to pay double the amount they were required to restore.
One should diligently restore stolen property in its original form;
in the absence of that, its value shall be paid, and a fine equal to that amount must be imposed.
Of wood, branches, grass, and the like, as well as those made of clay;
of bamboo and articles made of bamboo, and of cane, sinew, bone, and leather.
In the case of stealing vegetables, greens, and roots, as well as fruits and flowers, and likewise dairy products, sugarcane derivatives, salt, and oil;
For cooked grains, prepared foods, intoxicants, and meat—
indeed for all items of low value— the fine shall be five times their price.
In the case of goods measured by weight, by liquid measure, or by number, as well as all those counted individually,
the fine shall be ten times their value if they are of superior quality.
For one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, Manu declared that one should be made to pay a fine eleven times the value.
For gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments and the most excellent gems, the punishment is death if the value exceeds one hundred [paṇas].
For one who abducts a man, the punishment shall be the highest amercement;
for one who abducts a woman, the forfeiture of all property; but for one who abducts a maiden, the penalty is death.
For one who steals large livestock, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for stealing medium-sized livestock, the middle amercement; and for stealing small livestock, the first amercement.
The former [minimum] shall be twenty-four, and the latter [maximum] ninety-six;
the middle [range] shall be five hundred at most and two hundred at least.
A fine of one thousand [paṇas] is to be known as the highest, while the lowest is five hundred;
thus has the threefold punishment for acts of violence been proclaimed by the Self-Existent One.
In the first case of breaking a knot, there shall be the cutting off of the finger and the thumb;
in the second case, the remainder of that [limb] shall be cut off, and the first amercement shall be the fine.
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, there shall be the cutting off of a large piece of flesh;

"By whatever specific limb a thief commits a violation, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the instruction of Manu."
Whether the offense is more serious or less serious, one should inflict a heavier punishment on a thief; it should not be the same as that for a first-time offender.

The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the two hands, and fifthly the two feet;

Having fully ascertained the offense according to its true nature, as well as the place and time, and having considered the gravity of the crime and the circumstances of the offender, he should impose these punishments.
A perpetrator of violence must not be released by the king on account of friendship or from the acquisition of vast wealth;
he should rather be abandoned [by the king], for Manu has declared that such a person has already sacrificed his own life.

As much demerit accrues to a king from executing one who should not be executed, so much does he incur from releasing one who deserves execution; yet, for him who restrains the wicked, there is merit.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in every kind of sin;
one may at will banish him—such is the settled law.
The king may either confiscate all his property or leave a fourth part remaining;
remembering the duty toward his dependents, he should follow the law of Prajāpati—this is the established rule.
But for a Brāhmaṇa’s offense, four marks are prescribed:
for violating the Guru’s bed, for drinking liquor, for theft, and for harming a Brāhmaṇa.
For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, a tavern-sign is prescribed.
For theft, however, having fashioned the footprint of a dog, one should brand it with the bile of a peacock.
A man who has killed an embryo must be branded on the forehead with the mark of a headless corpse;
furthermore, he must be excluded from social intercourse—this is the instruction of Manu.
A thief must go before the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I have done this; punish me."
By this act, he becomes a thief because of the execution of his own deed;
that guilt shall touch the king who releases him while he is still stained by sin.
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his guilt;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked;
and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the instructor for those whose sins are concealed.
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra amounts to eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is twice eightfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
"Sixty-four [years] for a Brāhmaṇa"—thus Svāyambhuva has declared;

Punishment is traditionally held to be of two kinds: corporal and pecuniary.
Corporal punishments are said to be tenfold, while pecuniary punishments are manifold.
The monetary fine begins with a *kākaṇī* and likewise ends with the confiscation of all one's property;
the corporal punishment, however, begins with confinement and likewise ends with the taking of life.
The fine beginning with one *kākaṇī* is recorded as ending at one *māṣa*;
while that which is declared to begin with one *māṣa* ends at one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
But [the fines] beginning with one *kārṣāpaṇa* and ending with four *kārṣāpaṇas*,
another beginning with two and ending with eight, and yet another beginning with three and ending with twelve.
All those [fines] beginning with the kārṣāpaṇa that have been mentioned shall each be quadrupled;
others, however, are to be understood in the same way, up to the first amercement (pūrvasāhasa).
In the southern direction, the silver kārṣāpaṇa circulates;

A *māṣa* should be known as one-twentieth of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;

In the region of the Five Rivers, however, there is a conventional designation;

A *kārṣāpaṇa* should be known as four *aṇḍikās*, and four of those make one *dhānaka*. Twelve of those [make] a *suvarṇa*; a *dīnāra* is recorded as being equal to a *citraka*.
